allen/montgomery-farm.tagline: Where Allen let the creek write the master plan
intro: Montgomery Farm was planned around a question most developments never ask: what if you built with the land instead of over it? The result is a creekside community in Allen where wooded corridors, native plantings, and preserved green space are part of the design, not an afterthought. It's eco-minded in the practical Texas sense — more shade and habitat, less turf grass pretending it enjoys August.

Life here trades a little suburban uniformity for a lot of texture. The creek corridor sets the neighborhood's pace, mornings come with actual birdsong, and the tree cover does real work in a North Texas summer. You're still fully connected — Watters Creek's shops and restaurants are close, US 75 keeps downtown Dallas about 31 minutes out, and Allen ISD serves the neighborhood — but the setting feels calmer and greener than the standard suburban grid.
allen/montgomery-farm.homes: Homes at Montgomery Farm reflect the community's environmental brief: thoughtful siting that keeps trees, designs oriented to shade and green views, and landscaping that leans native rather than nursery-standard. Architecture skews considered rather than cookie-cutter — this isn't a place where the same elevation repeats down the block. Lots range from garden-scaled to creekside settings with real woods past the fence line. It suits buyers who want a neighborhood with a point of view: people who'd choose tree canopy over a fourth garage bay, and who like that the community's greenest feature is the land it kept.

highlights.title: Creekside setting
highlights.note: The community follows a creek corridor, with woods and green space woven into the plan.

highlights.title: Eco-minded design
highlights.note: Native landscaping and preserved land — sustainability as the founding idea, not a retrofit.

highlights.title: Near Watters Creek
highlights.note: Allen's open-air shopping and dining district sits close by for easy evenings out.

highlights.title: Connected calm
highlights.note: A quieter, greener pocket that still reaches US 75 and the city's amenities in minutes.

faq.q: Who is Montgomery Farm right for?
faq.a: If the standard North Texas subdivision feels a little too paved, Montgomery Farm is the counterargument. The community was designed around its creek and tree cover, so daily life comes with shade, green views, and a setting most suburbs can't offer. You keep Allen's practical advantages — Allen ISD, nearby shopping, highway access — while living somewhere that feels genuinely different.

faq.q: What makes Montgomery Farm eco-friendly?
faq.a: The community was planned with conservation in mind from the start: preserved creekside land, native plantings, and development that works around the existing tree cover instead of clearing it. In practice that means more shade, more habitat, and a landscape that handles Texas weather more gracefully than wall-to-wall turf. It's an ethos you can see from the street.

faq.q: What school district serves Montgomery Farm?
faq.a: Montgomery Farm is served by Allen ISD, the one-high-school district that gives Allen its distinctive all-in civic identity. Students here follow the same path as every other kid in the city, which keeps school communities unified and makes Friday night football something close to a municipal holiday.

faq.q: Can you commute to Dallas or Fort Worth from Montgomery Farm?
faq.a: Count on about 31 minutes to downtown Dallas and about 50 to downtown Fort Worth. The nearer numbers matter more day to day: Legacy West in Plano is roughly 12 minutes and DFW Airport about 30, putting the region's big job centers within a comfortable radius of the neighborhood.

faq.q: Are there new construction homes in Montgomery Farm?
faq.a: Availability shifts with the market, but Montgomery Farm is a largely developed community, so most listings are resale. Given the design-forward, land-first character here, resale is no downgrade — you're buying into mature plantings and a proven setting. Buyers focused on brand-new construction usually widen the search to actively building communities elsewhere in the DFW area.

allen/starcreek.tagline: Where north Allen dresses up without losing the commute
intro: StarCreek sits on Allen's north side, close enough to SH 121 that the whole corridor — Legacy West, the corporate campuses, the airport run — feels like an extension of the neighborhood. It's one of the city's newer upscale communities, and it reads that way: bigger elevations, fresher streetscapes, and the kind of polish that comes from a master plan built in one confident stretch rather than accreted over decades.

Living here is efficient in a way North Texas does well. Legacy West is about 12 minutes, DFW Airport about 30, and downtown Dallas about 31, so two-career households can split commutes in different directions without anyone drawing the short straw. Between drives, Allen's full suburban toolkit — shopping, restaurants, parks, and everything else along the 121 corridor — carries the weekends without much windshield time.
allen/starcreek.homes: This is Allen's newer-luxury tier: stone-and-brick elevations with real presence, open layouts designed for how people actually live now, and finish levels a clear step above the standard suburban spec. Lots are landscaped to the master plan's standard, so streets feel cohesive rather than patchwork. StarCreek suits move-up buyers and relocating professionals who want newer construction quality near the 121 corridor without committing to a build timeline — the homes are recent enough to feel current but established enough that the neighborhood already works.

highlights.title: 121 corridor access
highlights.note: SH 121 puts Legacy West about 12 minutes away and DFW Airport about 30.

highlights.title: Newer luxury stock
highlights.note: Recent-vintage homes with upscale elevations and current layouts — Allen's polished tier.

highlights.title: Master-plan cohesion
highlights.note: Built in one planned stretch, so streetscapes and landscaping feel deliberately consistent.

highlights.title: One-team schools
highlights.note: Students feed into Allen ISD and its famous single-high-school tradition.

faq.q: Is StarCreek a good place to live?
faq.a: StarCreek works well for buyers who want newer, higher-end suburban housing with a serious commute advantage. The neighborhood sits near SH 121 on Allen's north side, so job centers along the corridor are minutes away, while Allen ISD and the city's parks-and-shopping infrastructure handle daily life. If your priorities are newer construction quality and location efficiency, it's a short list and StarCreek is on it.

faq.q: Which school district covers StarCreek?
faq.a: StarCreek is zoned to Allen ISD, the single-high-school district that gives the city its one-town, one-team identity. For families relocating from out of state, that structure is unusual and genuinely useful — no boundary lotteries between rival high schools, just one program the entire city funds and follows together.

faq.q: Are there new construction homes in StarCreek?
faq.a: StarCreek's original build-out is largely complete, so most opportunities are recent-vintage resales rather than new builds. For many buyers that's the sweet spot: newer homes with the landscaping grown in and the neighborhood running smoothly, minus the wait and decision fatigue of a from-scratch build. Buyers wanting brand-new typically look to actively developing communities elsewhere in the northern DFW corridor.

faq.q: What are commutes like from StarCreek?
faq.a: Downtown Dallas is about 31 minutes and downtown Fort Worth about 50, but StarCreek's real advantage is the near field: Legacy West in Plano runs about 12 minutes and DFW Airport about 30 via SH 121. Most residents here point their commutes at the corridor rather than the downtowns.

faq.q: What is near StarCreek in Allen?
faq.a: The SH 121 corridor is the headline — shopping, dining, and quick highway movement in every direction. Allen's own amenities, from Watters Creek's restaurants to the city's park system, are a short drive away, and the broader corridor keeps adding retail and employers, which is part of why north Allen keeps attracting move-up buyers.

allen/twin-creeks.tagline: Fairways, greenbelts, and west Allen's most settled address
intro: Twin Creeks is what most people picture when they hear 'west Allen': a golf course threading between subdivisions, greenbelt trails stitching the sections together, and streets shaded by trees that were planted long enough ago to mean it. This is a master plan that has fully grown into itself — the landscaping has stopped arguing with the North Texas sun, and the neighbors know which cul-de-sac hosts the big Fourth of July cookout.

Daily life here runs on short loops. Watters Creek's restaurants and shops handle most weekend errands, Legacy West in Plano is about 12 minutes when the commute calls, and both US 75 and SH 121 are close without being audible. Allen ISD covers the neighborhood, the golf course anchors the social calendar, and the trail network means an evening walk doesn't require a car ride first.
allen/twin-creeks.homes: The housing stock spans a wide arc for one neighborhood: tidy brick traditionals on interior streets, roomier two-stories along the greenbelts, and larger custom-leaning homes backing the fairways. Lots feel established — mature trees, real setbacks, landscaping that has had years of attention. Architecture leans classic North Texas brick-and-stone rather than anything trendy, which keeps the streetscape coherent. Twin Creeks suits buyers who want Allen's west side with the golf-course address: move-up families, golfers, and anyone who'd rather inherit mature shade than wait fifteen years for saplings.

highlights.title: Golf-course spine
highlights.note: The course winds through the neighborhood, giving whole sections fairway views and a built-in social hub.

highlights.title: Greenbelt trails
highlights.note: Connected paths link sections, parks, and ponds — evening walks without leaving the neighborhood.

highlights.title: Quick highway access
highlights.note: US 75 and SH 121 are minutes away; Legacy West is about 12 minutes.

highlights.title: Allen ISD schools
highlights.note: The neighborhood feeds Allen ISD, the single-high-school district the whole town rallies behind.

faq.q: Who is Twin Creeks right for?
faq.a: If you want an established golf-course neighborhood in Allen, it's hard to argue with. Twin Creeks offers mature trees, connected trails, a range of home sizes, and a west-side location that keeps both US 75 and SH 121 in easy reach. It's a settled community rather than a construction zone, which is exactly the appeal for most buyers here.

faq.q: What are the schools for Twin Creeks?
faq.a: Twin Creeks is served by Allen ISD, the district famous for running one giant high school for the entire city. In practice that means every kid in the neighborhood grows up wearing the same colors as the rest of Allen — a one-town, one-team setup that does a lot of the community-building on its own.

faq.q: How far is Twin Creeks from downtown Dallas or Fort Worth?
faq.a: Downtown Dallas runs about 31 minutes from Allen via US 75, and downtown Fort Worth is about 50. Closer to home, Legacy West in Plano is roughly 12 minutes and DFW Airport about 30, which is the math that matters for most people working the corporate corridors of the northern suburbs.

faq.q: Can you buy new construction in Twin Creeks?
faq.a: Twin Creeks is essentially built out, so the market here is resale rather than new construction. That's a feature for many buyers: you can see exactly how the neighborhood aged, and it aged well. Buyers set on brand-new homes usually look to Allen's newer communities or master plans farther up the DFW growth corridor.

faq.q: Do homes in Twin Creeks back to the golf course?
faq.a: Some do — the course threads through the neighborhood, so certain streets back directly to fairways while others face greenbelts or interior lots. Golf-course lots typically carry a premium and move quickly when they list. If a fairway view is the goal, tell your agent early; if you just want the setting, plenty of homes get the benefit without the stray golf balls.

allen/watters-crossing.tagline: The Allen neighborhood that can walk to dinner
intro: Most North Texas suburbs make you drive for everything; Watters Crossing quietly opted out. The neighborhood sits within walking distance of Watters Creek, Allen's open-air shopping and dining district, which means Friday dinner, Saturday coffee, and an impulse ice cream run can all happen on foot. It's an established community with sidewalks that actually go somewhere — a rarity worth naming in this part of Collin County.

The rest of the ledger is classic Allen: mature trees over established streets, Allen ISD for the school-age crowd, and US 75 close by for commutes — downtown Dallas is about 31 minutes, Legacy West about 12. Weeknights, you'll see the neighborhood out on those sidewalks, headed toward the green at Watters Creek or just making laps. It's suburban living with the car keys optional more often than usual.
allen/watters-crossing.homes: Watters Crossing is established brick suburbia done properly: traditional one- and two-story homes on streets where the trees have caught up with the rooflines. Floor plans are the practical kind — formal dining that became the office, living areas that open to real backyards. Nothing here is trying to be new; the appeal is exactly the opposite. It suits families who want walkable Allen without the wait of new construction, and buyers who'd trade builder-fresh finishes for location, shade, and a neighborhood that already knows itself.

highlights.title: Walk to Watters Creek
highlights.note: Restaurants, shops, and the open-air green are sidewalk distance from much of the neighborhood.

highlights.title: Established tree canopy
highlights.note: Mature shade and settled landscaping — the payoff of an older-vintage Allen neighborhood.

highlights.title: US 75 nearby
highlights.note: Straight shot to downtown Dallas in about 31 minutes; Legacy West about 12.

highlights.title: Allen ISD zoned
highlights.note: Kids join the one-high-school pipeline the whole city shows up for on Fridays.

faq.q: What is it like to live in Watters Crossing?
faq.a: For buyers who value walkability, it's one of Allen's best answers. Watters Crossing pairs an established neighborhood feel — mature trees, sidewalks, settled streets — with sidewalk access to Watters Creek's restaurants and shopping. Add Allen ISD and quick US 75 access, and it covers the fundamentals most families are actually shopping for in North Texas.

faq.q: What school district serves Watters Crossing?
faq.a: Watters Crossing is served by Allen ISD. The district runs a single high school for the whole city — a deliberate one-town, one-team model — so kids from this neighborhood grow up in the same pipeline as everyone else in Allen, from elementary through Friday nights at the stadium.

faq.q: Can you walk to Watters Creek from Watters Crossing?
faq.a: That's the neighborhood's signature. Watters Creek — Allen's open-air district of restaurants, shops, and green space — sits within walking distance, so dinner out doesn't automatically mean driving. Exact walk times vary by street, but the sidewalk connections make it a genuine everyday amenity rather than a marketing line.

faq.q: How long is the drive to downtown Dallas or Fort Worth from Watters Crossing?
faq.a: Downtown Dallas is about 31 minutes via US 75, which runs right past this side of Allen, and downtown Fort Worth is about 50. Legacy West in Plano is roughly 12 minutes and DFW Airport about 30 — commute math that works for most jobs along the northern corridor.

faq.q: Are there new construction homes in Watters Crossing?
faq.a: No — Watters Crossing is an established, built-out neighborhood, and that's the point. The market here is resale: homes with mature landscaping and a track record. Buyers occasionally find updated or renovated listings, which can deliver a nearly-new interior in a location no new community can replicate — walking distance to Watters Creek.

anna/anacapri.tagline: Beach-day living arrives at Collin County's front-door price
intro: Anacapri is the newcomer that made the rest of Anna look up: a master-planned community built around a swimmable crystal lagoon, now selling on the north end of the US-75 corridor. The pitch is simple and a little audacious — resort-style water in a town known for practical starter homes. Five builders are working the early phases, and the streets still have that fresh-poured optimism where every second yard sign says welcome home.

Living here means the lagoon is the default answer to summer. Instead of loading the car for a splurge weekend, you walk down for a swim and sand between your toes, then head home for dinner. Beyond the water, it is new-community life in fast-growing North Texas: neighbors comparing floor plans, schools running through Anna ISD, and Legacy West in Plano about 30 minutes south when the workweek calls.
anna/anacapri.homes: Everything in Anacapri is new construction, with five builders offering distinct plan lines and pricing that starts from the $360s — genuinely rare for a lagoon community anywhere in DFW, let alone Collin County. Expect the full modern production playbook: open-concept mains, flex rooms doing double duty as offices, and elevations that mix brick, stone, and board-and-batten. Lots run compact, which is part of how the math works; the lagoon is the backyard upgrade. It suits first-time buyers stretching into something memorable, and move-up families who want amenities their previous starter neighborhood never had.

highlights.title: Crystal lagoon
highlights.note: A swimmable lagoon anchors the community — beach days without the beach drive.

highlights.title: Five builders
highlights.note: Multiple plan lines selling now, from compact starters to roomier footprints.

highlights.title: Entry pricing
highlights.note: New construction from the $360s — Collin County's ground floor.

highlights.title: Anna ISD
highlights.note: Schools run through Anna ISD — verify assignments by address with the district.

faq.q: What is it like to live in Anacapri?
faq.a: If you want a brand-new home with a genuine centerpiece amenity, Anacapri is one of the more interesting bets in North Texas right now. The lagoon gives it an identity most entry-priced communities lack, and Anna's US-75 access keeps commutes workable. Just go in knowing it is early days — construction traffic and unfinished phases are part of the deal for the first wave of residents.

faq.q: Can you buy new construction in Anacapri?
faq.a: Yes — Anacapri is entirely new construction and currently selling, with five builders offering homes from the $360s. That gives buyers real choice in floor plans and finish styles within a single community. You can typically pick between inventory homes ready sooner and to-be-built homes where you select the lot and design options, so timelines range from weeks to the better part of a year.

faq.q: What is inside Anacapri?
faq.a: The headliner is the crystal lagoon — a swimmable, beach-entry body of water that functions as the community's shared backyard, with sand and lounging space along the shore. Supporting amenities are built around it: gathering areas, green space, and paths that make walking to the water the default. As with any new community, amenities open in phases, so ask what is complete versus planned.

faq.q: What are the schools for Anacapri?
faq.a: Anacapri is served by Anna ISD. Because the community is new and the district is growing alongside the city, campus assignments can change as boundaries are drawn for future schools — verify the current zoning with Anna ISD when you contract, and ask your builder's sales office what they are telling other buyers.

faq.q: What are commutes like from Anacapri?
faq.a: Downtown Dallas runs about 50 minutes via US-75, and downtown Fort Worth is the long haul at about 66 minutes. More relevant for most households: Legacy West in Plano is about 30 minutes, and DFW Airport about 45. Anna trades a longer core-city commute for a price of entry that closer suburbs stopped offering years ago.

faq.q: How competitive is Anacapri right now?
faq.a: Anna's US-75 corridor is one of the metro's fastest-growing, and Anacapri's lagoon at a $360s entry is the local conversation piece. Pricing and releases change quickly — verify current availability with the sales offices.

faq.q: What should I compare Anacapri against?
faq.a: Churchill and Parks at Foster Crossing, both in Anna, compete in the same band without the lagoon. EastRidge in Princeton is the value alternative one corridor east — the Anna guide on this site maps all of it.

amenities: Swimmable crystal lagoon at the center of the community
Sand-beach shoreline for lounging and lagoon days
Walking paths connecting streets to the water
Community green spaces threaded between phases
buyerNotes: Anacapri is selling in phases, and early phases usually carry the sharpest pricing — builders reward buyers who commit before the amenity is fully proven. Ask each sales office how lot releases are staggered and when the lagoon itself is scheduled to open.

Lots near the lagoon or facing green space typically carry premiums. Decide early whether location or finishes matter more — both pull from the same budget, and a base-price home on a premium lot often holds value better than an upgraded home on a standard one.

Amenity-rich communities fund their amenities through the HOA, and a lagoon is not a cheap thing to maintain. Before contracting, get the current dues, what they cover, and any access or guest policies in writing — then budget design-center spending after those numbers, not before.

anna/sherley-farms.tagline: New streets growing up alongside Anna's original downtown grid
intro: Most of Anna's new construction pushes toward the edges; Sherley Farms went the other direction. Its phases are opening close to downtown Anna, which means buying brand-new without exiling yourself from the oldest, most walkable part of town. As the city works to fill its historic core with the restaurants and retail all these rooftops are demanding, Sherley Farms residents are positioned to be regulars from day one.

Day to day, that geography is the neighborhood's quiet advantage. School runs stay short inside Anna ISD, US-75 is close enough for a Plano commute of about 30 minutes to Legacy West, and errands do not require a highway. The community itself has the energy of a place mid-build — new families arriving in waves, fresh sod going down, and phase maps posted where finished streets will eventually run.
anna/sherley-farms.homes: Sherley Farms is new-construction territory with phases still opening, so buyers get the full menu: inventory homes ready soon, to-be-built contracts with lot selection, and floor plans that lean into the current North Texas playbook — open living areas, kitchen islands built for homework, and flexible fourth bedrooms. Elevations run traditional brick with stone accents, and lots are sized for easy weekend maintenance rather than serious acreage. It suits buyers who want a warranty and modern systems but also want downtown Anna's coffee-and-errands orbit close by, instead of a thirty-minute round trip for a gallon of milk.

highlights.title: Downtown adjacency
highlights.note: Anna's original town grid — and its growing storefront scene — is minutes away.

highlights.title: Active phases
highlights.note: New sections keep opening, so lot and plan choice stays wide.

highlights.title: New-build systems
highlights.note: Modern construction, warranties, and energy standards without leaving the town core.

faq.q: Who is Sherley Farms right for?
faq.a: It makes a strong case for buyers who want new construction with a sense of place. Living near downtown Anna means the town's oldest streets and its newest investment are both on your doorstep, and the commute math works: US-75 nearby, Legacy West in Plano about 30 minutes. The honest caveat is construction — active phases mean builder traffic until the community finishes out.

faq.q: Can you buy new construction in Sherley Farms?
faq.a: Yes. Sherley Farms is actively building, with new phases opening near downtown Anna. That typically means a mix of move-in-ready inventory homes and to-be-built options where you choose the lot and finishes. Availability shifts quickly in communities at this stage, so check current phase maps and release schedules with the onsite sales teams rather than relying on listing portals.

faq.q: What school district serves Sherley Farms?
faq.a: Sherley Farms is served by Anna ISD. The neighborhood's near-downtown location keeps it close to the district's established heart, though as Anna grows, boundaries get revisited — new campuses tend to follow new rooftops. Confirm the current campus assignments with Anna ISD during your option period so there are no surprises at enrollment time.

faq.q: Can you commute to Dallas or Fort Worth from Sherley Farms?
faq.a: From Sherley Farms, downtown Dallas is about 50 minutes via US-75 and downtown Fort Worth about 66 — Fort Worth commuters should test-drive that one before committing. The friendlier numbers: Legacy West in Plano at about 30 minutes and DFW Airport at about 45, which covers a large share of North Texas jobs.

anna/villages-of-hurricane-creek.tagline: Bigger lots and slower rhythms off FM 455
intro: Follow FM 455 out from Anna's core and the town starts to loosen its collar — that is where the Villages of Hurricane Creek sits. The community borrows its name from the creek threading this side of Collin County, and borrows its character from lots that give production homes something rare at this price point: honest breathing room between you and the neighbors.

Life here trades a little convenience for a lot of elbow room. You will drive for groceries and for US-75, but you get evenings where the loudest thing on the street is a lawnmower winding down. Kids attend Anna ISD, trucks and trailers actually fit on the driveways, and the sky still does that big North Texas thing at sunset. For buyers who moved to Anna to feel less stacked-up, this is the neighborhood that delivers on it.
anna/villages-of-hurricane-creek.homes: Housing in the Villages of Hurricane Creek follows the larger-lot brief: single-family homes with wider frontages, deeper backyards, and side yards that read as usable space instead of a drainage easement. Architecture stays North Texas traditional — brick and stone elevations, covered patios, three-car garages appearing more often than elsewhere in Anna. The buyer it suits is specific: someone who wants room for a garden, a shop bench, or a dog with real acreage ambitions, and who will happily trade walkable retail for that. It also draws move-up buyers leaving tighter starter streets without leaving Anna ISD.

highlights.title: Larger lots
highlights.note: Wider frontages and deeper yards than Anna's typical starter streets.

highlights.title: FM 455 access
highlights.note: One road connects you back to US-75 and the rest of town.

highlights.title: Creek-country setting
highlights.note: Named for Hurricane Creek, with the open feel to match.

highlights.title: Anna ISD
highlights.note: Served by Anna ISD like the rest of the city.

faq.q: Is Villages of Hurricane Creek a good place to live?
faq.a: For space-first buyers, yes — this is where Anna's larger lots live, and the difference is obvious the moment you turn off FM 455. The trade-offs are the usual ones: you are farther from US-75 and daily retail than neighborhoods near the highway, and quiet is the amenity rather than a pool or a lagoon. Buyers tend to self-select accordingly.

faq.q: What are lot sizes like in Villages of Hurricane Creek?
faq.a: Larger than Anna's norm — that is the community's calling card. Instead of quoting numbers that vary lot to lot, think in terms of what fits: wider side yards, deeper backyards, and driveways that hold more than two vehicles. Individual listings will spell out exact dimensions, and they differ enough between sections that it is worth comparing several before you commit.

faq.q: Which school district covers Villages of Hurricane Creek?
faq.a: The community is zoned to Anna ISD, the same district serving the rest of the city. Anna ISD's footprint covers a fast-growing area, which means attendance zones evolve as campuses are added — a quick call to the district with a specific address is the reliable way to confirm current assignments before making an offer.

faq.q: What are commutes like from Villages of Hurricane Creek?
faq.a: Budget about 50 minutes to downtown Dallas and about 66 to downtown Fort Worth, with FM 455 carrying you to US-75 first. Legacy West in Plano sits about 30 minutes out and DFW Airport about 45. The lot size is what you are buying with those minutes — most residents here consider it a fair exchange.

anna/west-crossing.tagline: Where Anna's boom first put down roots and lawns
intro: West Crossing is what Anna looked like before the cranes showed up in force — an early master-planned neighborhood on the west side of US-75 where the trees have caught up to the rooflines and the sidewalks carry real foot traffic. For buyers who like the price of a fast-growing North Texas town but not the mud of an active construction phase, this is the settled option: streets that are finished, neighbors who are staying.

Daily life here runs on simple geometry. US-75 is a few minutes east, which puts Legacy West in Plano about 30 minutes away and downtown Dallas at about 50. Kids walk or ride to Anna ISD campuses, evenings mean garage-door conversations and youth-sports carpools, and weekends drift toward downtown Anna's slowly filling storefronts. It is starter-home country in the best sense — a place people land on purpose and then decide not to leave.
anna/west-crossing.homes: The housing stock in West Crossing is classic North Texas starter fare: one- and two-story production homes with brick-and-stone fronts, practical three- and four-bedroom layouts, and lots sized for a swing set rather than a tractor. Because the neighborhood went in ahead of Anna's newest wave, most of what trades here is resale — which means established landscaping, finished fences, and no design-center decisions. It suits first-time buyers who want move-in-ready over brand-new, and anyone priced out of communities farther down US-75 who still wants Collin County on the address line.

highlights.title: Settled streets
highlights.note: Finished blocks, grown-in lawns, and neighbors past the moving-box stage.

highlights.title: US-75 at hand
highlights.note: The highway sits minutes east, running straight toward Plano and Dallas.

highlights.title: Anna ISD
highlights.note: The neighborhood is served by Anna ISD, with campuses close to home.

highlights.title: Resale ready
highlights.note: Move-in-ready homes without new-construction wait times or upgrade sticker shock.

faq.q: Is West Crossing a good place to live?
faq.a: For first-time buyers and young families, it is one of Anna's most sensible landings. The neighborhood is established rather than under construction, US-75 is close for commuting, and the price of entry sits below most of Collin County. The trade-off is that Anna's retail and restaurant scene is still catching up to its rooftops — though the city is actively working on that.

faq.q: Which school district covers West Crossing?
faq.a: West Crossing is zoned to Anna ISD, the district serving the city of Anna. In a town growing this fast, attendance boundaries can and do get redrawn as new campuses come online, so it is worth confirming current school assignments directly with Anna ISD before you write an offer.

faq.q: How long is the drive to downtown Dallas or Fort Worth from West Crossing?
faq.a: Plan on about 50 minutes to downtown Dallas straight down US-75, and about 66 minutes to downtown Fort Worth. Closer-in job centers are the everyday story: Legacy West in Plano runs about 30 minutes, and DFW Airport is about 45. For a Collin County address at Anna's prices, that Plano commute is the number most buyers care about.

faq.q: Are homes in West Crossing new construction or resale?
faq.a: Mostly resale. West Crossing is one of Anna's earlier master-planned neighborhoods, so the streets are largely built out and homes come to market the traditional way — with sellers, established yards, and window coverings already hung. Buyers set on brand-new construction usually look at Anna's newer communities instead, while West Crossing draws people who would rather skip the build timeline.

argyle/5t-ranch.tagline: Estate lots where Argyle still stretches its legs
intro: On the east side of Argyle, 5T Ranch is what people picture when they say they're moving out here for land: custom homes set back on estate lots, long views between houses, and streets quiet enough to hear a horse trailer coming. It's Argyle in its classic register — unhurried, spread out, and unapologetically residential — with the town's small-district schools anchoring the appeal for families.

The east-side position matters for commuters. You get the acreage lifestyle without surrendering the workweek — downtown Dallas runs about 44 minutes, DFW Airport about 28, and downtown Fort Worth about 34. Evenings and weekends belong to the lot: kids with room to roam, dogs with actual jobs, and sunsets you can see all the way down. For a lot of North Texas buyers, that trade is the whole point.
argyle/5t-ranch.homes: 5T Ranch homes are custom by nature — stone-and-brick traditionals, Texas transitional designs, and modern-farmhouse builds, each shaped to its own lot rather than stamped from a plan book. Expect long driveways, side-entry garages, and backyards with room for a pool, a shop, or both. The estate-lot scale means maintenance is a lifestyle decision, not an afterthought: you'll want a mower you can sit on. It suits move-up and forever-home buyers who want land, privacy, and Argyle ISD without taking on a full working ranch.

highlights.title: Estate-scale lots
highlights.note: Room between houses is the defining feature — privacy comes standard, not as an upgrade.

highlights.title: Custom architecture
highlights.note: No two builds alike; homes were designed to their lots, not repeated down the street.

highlights.title: East-side access
highlights.note: Positioned on Argyle's Dallas-facing side, which shaves real time off eastbound commutes.

highlights.title: Argyle ISD
highlights.note: The small district that draws families to town serves this side of it too.

faq.q: Is 5T Ranch a good place to live?
faq.a: For buyers who define quality of life in square feet of sky, absolutely. 5T Ranch delivers the estate-lot version of Argyle — quiet, roomy, custom-built — while staying close enough to the east-side corridors that commuting stays realistic. It's not the neighborhood for people who want walkable retail or a packed amenity calendar; the amenity here is the land itself.

faq.q: Which school district covers 5T Ranch?
faq.a: 5T Ranch is in Argyle ISD, the small Denton County district whose reputation does a lot of heavy lifting in local real-estate decisions. Families frequently pick Argyle specifically for the district, and estate neighborhoods like this one are a big part of how they get here. As always, confirm campus assignments for a specific address with the district itself.

faq.q: How long is the drive to downtown Dallas or Fort Worth from 5T Ranch?
faq.a: Plan on about 44 minutes to downtown Dallas and about 34 to downtown Fort Worth, with DFW Airport closer at about 28. The east-side location helps anyone heading toward Dallas or the airport. Like anywhere in North Texas, rush hour writes its own schedule, so test-drive your actual commute at your actual hour before committing.

faq.q: What kind of homes are in 5T Ranch?
faq.a: Custom single-family homes on estate lots — think stone and brick exteriors, generous footprints, and floor plans designed for the specific parcel rather than repeated by a production builder. Outdoor living is a major theme: covered patios, room for pools, and yards that justify the drive. Availability is resale-driven, so inventory comes and goes; patience tends to be rewarded here.

argyle/country-lakes.tagline: Sidewalk suburbia in a town built on acreage
intro: Country Lakes is Argyle's more conventional neighborhood — family-scaled streets off FM 407 where the houses sit closer together, the sidewalks connect, and kids actually know each other's garage codes. In a town famous for acre-plus custom estates, that makes it something of an outlier, and a useful one: it's the front door to Argyle for households who want the town without the tractor.

The 407 address earns its keep. That corridor puts groceries, school runs, and both sides of the Metroplex within easy reach — about 28 minutes to DFW Airport and about 34 to downtown Fort Worth or Legacy West in Plano. Daily life leans practical and social: bikes in driveways, neighbors on first-name terms, and weekend schedules organized around Argyle ISD calendars more than anything else.
argyle/country-lakes.homes: Expect established production-built single-family homes on suburban-scale lots — brick-heavy elevations, two-car garages, and floor plans built for the school-age years. Compared with Argyle's estate neighborhoods, yards here are manageable rather than monumental, which is exactly the appeal for a lot of buyers. This is one of the more attainable ways into Argyle ISD, and resale activity reflects that: family buyers circling the same streets for the same reasons. It suits first-time and move-up households who'd rather spend Saturday at the ballfield than on a zero-turn mower.

highlights.title: FM 407 convenience
highlights.note: The corridor handles errands, school runs, and highway connections without much drama.

highlights.title: Family-scaled streets
highlights.note: Sidewalks, closer lots, and a critical mass of kids — built for bikes and block parties.

highlights.title: Attainable Argyle
highlights.note: One of the town's more approachable entry points for getting into Argyle ISD.

highlights.title: Manageable yards
highlights.note: Suburban lots mean weekend upkeep stays a chore, not a second career.

faq.q: Why do people choose Country Lakes?
faq.a: For families, it's one of the easiest yeses in Argyle. Country Lakes trades the town's signature acreage for connected streets, nearby conveniences along FM 407, and neighbors close enough to borrow from. You give up the big-lot privacy that defines much of Argyle, but you gain a neighborhood that actually functions like one — and a lighter maintenance load.

faq.q: What are the schools for Country Lakes?
faq.a: Country Lakes sits within Argyle ISD, and for many buyers that's the beginning and end of the search criteria. The district's small size means the schools function as the town's social hub, and neighborhoods like this one feed directly into that rhythm. Confirm current campus assignments with the district for any specific address, since boundaries can shift as the area grows.

faq.q: What new homes are available in Country Lakes?
faq.a: Country Lakes is an established neighborhood, so most opportunities come through resale rather than builder contracts. That's not a drawback — you can see exactly how the streets have matured, and you skip the construction-zone years. Buyers set on brand-new in the Argyle area usually look at Harvest, the master plan on the town's west side that's now selling its final phase.

faq.q: How far is Country Lakes from downtown Dallas or Fort Worth?
faq.a: Figure about 44 minutes to downtown Dallas and about 34 to downtown Fort Worth, with DFW Airport the shortest big commute at about 28 minutes. The FM 407 location makes reaching either side of the region straightforward. As with any North Texas drive, those numbers stretch during peak hours, so it's worth running the route at your real departure time before you commit.

argyle/harvest.tagline: Where the HOA runs a farmstand and means it
intro: Harvest took the farm theme seriously. This master-planned community on Argyle's western edge — spilling across the line into Northlake — is built around a working community garden and a farmstand that sells what the neighborhood grows. It's one of North Texas's better-known master plans, and it earned that by giving people something to do together: seasonal events, garden plots, and a calendar that revolves around the dirt as much as the pool.

Day to day, it reads as friendly and busy. Kids ride bikes to the trails, someone's always at the garden beds, and the drive to work is manageable — about 28 minutes to DFW Airport and about 34 to downtown Fort Worth. With the community now in its last sections, the streets feel settled rather than half-built, which is a rare mood for new construction in this part of DFW.
argyle/harvest.homes: Housing in Harvest runs the master-plan range: tidy cottage-scale plans up through roomier two-story family homes, most wearing some version of the modern-farmhouse look — board-and-batten, deep porches, black-framed windows. Lots are suburban-scaled, designed for porch-sitting more than pasture-keeping, which sets Harvest apart from Argyle's acreage tradition. New construction is still available in the closing sections from the $450s — verify phase status with the builders, alongside young resales throughout earlier sections. It suits buyers who want new-build convenience and a genuinely social street — and who'd rather join a garden than maintain an acre of one.

highlights.title: Community farmstand
highlights.note: Produce grown on-site ends up at the neighborhood stand — the farm theme is literal, not decorative.

highlights.title: Final-phase new builds
highlights.note: New construction from the $450s as Harvest closes out its last sections.

highlights.title: Two-town address
highlights.note: The community spans Argyle and Northlake, so verify which side a given street sits on.

highlights.title: Built-in social calendar
highlights.note: Garden plots, trails, and seasonal events keep neighbors bumping into each other on purpose.

faq.q: Why do people choose Harvest?
faq.a: If you want a new-construction neighborhood with an actual personality, yes. Harvest's garden-and-farmstand identity gives it more community texture than the average North Texas master plan, and the location west of Argyle proper keeps commutes reasonable — about 28 minutes to DFW Airport. The trade-off is master-plan living: closer neighbors, HOA structure, and amenity dues rather than acreage independence.

faq.q: Is anyone still building in Harvest?
faq.a: Yes, though the window is closing. Harvest is selling its last sections, with new homes offered from the $450s — verify what remains with the builders. That means less lot selection than earlier phases but fully built-out amenities from day one. Buyers who miss the last new releases will still find young resales throughout the community, many only a few years lived-in.

faq.q: Is Harvest in Argyle or Northlake?
faq.a: Both. Harvest spans the boundary between Argyle and Northlake, so two neighbors can share a fence and different mailing addresses. For most daily purposes it functions as one community with one set of amenities. If the specific town matters to you — for taxes, services, or school attendance — confirm the exact parcel with your agent before you get attached to a floor plan.

faq.q: Which school district covers Harvest?
faq.a: Argyle ISD is the district associated with the Argyle side of Harvest, and it's a major reason families shop here — the district's reputation carries real weight in Denton County. Because the community crosses city lines, though, district boundaries don't always follow your assumptions. Verify the assigned campuses for any specific address directly with the district before making an offer.

faq.q: What amenities does Harvest have?
faq.a: The headliners are the community garden and the farmstand, where neighborhood-grown produce actually gets sold — the farm branding isn't just a sales-office mural. Around that core you'll find walking trails, gathering spaces, and a steady calendar of seasonal events. It's the kind of amenity set built for regular use rather than the occasional pool day, which shapes who the community attracts.

faq.q: How much longer will Harvest have new homes?
faq.a: Harvest is winding down its last sections, so remaining new-construction picks are the closeout kind — fewer lots, but builders tend to negotiate at this stage. Verify current phase status with the sales offices.

faq.q: What should I compare Harvest against?
faq.a: Pecan Square in Northlake is the natural cross-shop — same 35W corridor, similar front-porch programming, still mid-plan. The Argyle guide on this site covers the town's acreage side if the farm theme is the draw.

buyerNotes: Final-phase shopping flips the usual script: amenities are finished and streets are proven, but lot selection is thin. Walk what's left in person, and ask each builder about completed inventory homes if you need a faster close.

Advertised base prices rarely match final contracts. Budget real margin for the design center, spend it on structural choices — extra windows, extended patios, gas lines — and save purely cosmetic upgrades for later, when you can shop them competitively.

Amenity-rich master plans carry HOA dues to match, and Harvest's programming is part of what you're paying for. Request the full fee schedule and covenant documents up front so the monthly math is settled before you write an offer.

seo.title: Harvest in Argyle, TX — Farm-Themed New Homes, Closing Out
seo.description: Harvest is Argyle's farm-themed plan in its closing stretch — community garden, farmstand, and the last new-home releases from the $450s.

argyle/old-town-argyle.tagline: Original acreage, old oaks, and no two lots alike
intro: Old Town Argyle is the part of town the rest of Argyle grew out from — original acreage parcels shaded by oaks that were mature before anyone thought to call this place a suburb. The streets don't follow a master plan because there never was one; properties took their shapes over decades, and the result is a texture no new development can print.

Living here means trading uniformity for character. Your neighbor might keep chickens; the house across the road might be a fresh custom rebuild on an old footprint. What holds it together is the shade, the quiet, and proximity to the middle of town — with Argyle ISD nearby and the wider DFW job map reachable, downtown Fort Worth at about 34 minutes and DFW Airport at about 28.
argyle/old-town-argyle.homes: The housing stock is genuinely mixed: older ranch-style homes that have been loved (or lightly neglected) for generations, thorough remodels, and new custom builds replacing what stood before. What buyers are really purchasing is the land — treed, established acreage in the heart of Argyle, the kind that doesn't get created anymore. That makes Old Town Argyle a favorite for two camps: renovators who want good bones under a great canopy, and custom-build clients hunting a lot with history instead of a blank field on the edge of North Texas.

highlights.title: Mature oak canopy
highlights.note: Shade you can't buy new — the trees predate the town's growth spurt entirely.

highlights.title: Original acreage
highlights.note: Established parcels with irregular shapes and real elbow room, not subdivided sameness.

highlights.title: Heart-of-town setting
highlights.note: Close to Argyle's original core, where the town still feels like a town.

highlights.title: Rebuild potential
highlights.note: Treed lots draw custom builders and renovators looking for land with a past.

faq.q: Why do people choose Old Town Argyle?
faq.a: If character ranks above convenience on your list, it's hard to beat. Old Town Argyle offers established acreage, deep shade, and a settled feel that newer subdivisions spend decades chasing. The trade-offs are real: older homes need attention, lots vary wildly, and nobody is polishing the edges for you. For a lot of buyers, that last part is a feature.

faq.q: What school district serves Old Town Argyle?
faq.a: This is Argyle ISD territory — fitting, since the district and the old town grew up together. The schools are the center of gravity for the whole community, and living in the original part of town keeps you close to that orbit. For any specific property, verify current campus assignments with the district, especially if a lot has been split or replatted.

faq.q: What kinds of homes are in Old Town Argyle?
faq.a: A little of everything, which is the point. You'll find original ranch houses under big trees, extensively remodeled homes, and brand-new custom builds on lots where something older came down. Because parcels here were never stamped out by a single developer, sizes, setbacks, and styles all vary — walk any candidate property carefully and read the survey before you fall for the trees.

faq.q: How far is Old Town Argyle from downtown Dallas or Fort Worth?
faq.a: Count on about 34 minutes to downtown Fort Worth and about 44 to downtown Dallas, with DFW Airport at about 28. The central Argyle location keeps both halves of the Metroplex reachable without living beside a highway. North Texas traffic rewards flexible schedules, though, so those figures assume you're not leaving at the worst possible moment.

arlington/entertainment-district.tagline: Fireworks over the backyard, kickoff within walking distance
intro: Most of North Texas experiences Arlington's Entertainment District from a parking lot; a modest number of locals actually live in it. AT&T Stadium, Globe Life Field, and Six Flags Over Texas cluster within walking distance of one another, and the residential streets around them absorb the spectacle — flyovers before kickoff, fireworks after home runs, coaster screams carried on a south wind. You stop noticing, then you start scheduling around it.

Daily life is more practical than the postcard suggests. Texas Live! covers dinner-and-a-game logistics, event-day traffic teaches you the back ways within a month, and non-event days are surprisingly ordinary — quiet streets, big skies, easy highway access. Downtown Fort Worth runs about 15 minutes and downtown Dallas about 22, so the district works as a commuter base, not just a bucket-list address for Cowboys season-ticket holders.
arlington/entertainment-district.homes: Housing here is a patchwork rather than a plan: established brick homes on older streets, townhome rows built for the walk-to-the-game crowd, and infill that arrives whenever the district adds another attraction. Lot sizes and conditions vary block to block, so this is a part of Arlington you shop street by street rather than by boundary line. The buyers it fits are specific — die-hard fans, people who want walkable entertainment in a metroplex built around driving, and investors who like being near where DFW throws its biggest parties. If you need silence on a fall Sunday, keep shopping south.

highlights.title: Walk to kickoff
highlights.note: Cowboys and Rangers home games without a parking pass or a shuttle.

highlights.title: Texas Live! nearby
highlights.note: Restaurants, bars, and watch parties a short stroll from the front door.

highlights.title: Six Flags weeknights
highlights.note: Season passes turn coasters and Hurricane Harbor into after-dinner plans.

highlights.title: Dead-center metroplex
highlights.note: About 15 minutes to downtown Fort Worth, about 22 to downtown Dallas.

faq.q: Why do people choose the Entertainment District?
faq.a: It depends entirely on your relationship with event noise. If walking to Rangers games and treating Texas Live! as your default dinner spot sounds like the whole point of Arlington, yes — few addresses in DFW deliver that. If you treasure quiet fall Sundays, the game-day rhythm will wear on you. Visit on an event day before deciding; the neighborhood shows its true self then.

faq.q: What is it like living near AT&T Stadium on game days?
faq.a: Loud, busy, and manageable once you learn the pattern. Traffic builds for hours before kickoff and drains slowly afterward, so residents plan errands around the event calendar the way coastal towns plan around tides. Locals figure out which streets stay passable, some turn driveways into game-day income, and most will admit the fireworks and flyovers never fully lose their charm.

faq.q: Which school district covers the Entertainment District?
faq.a: The residential streets around the stadiums are served by Arlington ISD. Because homes here scatter across several pockets rather than one contiguous subdivision, campus assignments can differ from block to block — confirm the specific zoning for any address with Arlington ISD before you commit. The district's boundary map, not a listing's claim, is the version to trust.

faq.q: How far is the Entertainment District from downtown Dallas or Fort Worth?
faq.a: Downtown Fort Worth is about 15 minutes and downtown Dallas about 22, with DFW Airport about 17 — the district sits close to the midpoint of the metroplex, which is exactly why the stadiums landed here in the first place. For commuters, that means you can work in either downtown without a punishing drive, event traffic permitting.

arlington/interlochen.tagline: Canal-back yards and Decembers the whole metroplex drives to see
intro: Interlochen is the Arlington neighborhood people know without knowing its name — the one with the canals, where every December the streets fill with slow-rolling cars admiring one of North Texas's longest-running holiday light traditions. The other eleven months are quieter and arguably better: waterways lace between backyards, mature trees close over the streets, and the resident ducks have opinions about your landscaping.

Day to day, it lives like classic established Arlington — kids on bikes, garage-sale weekends, neighbors who have been here long enough to remember when the trees were saplings. The middle-of-the-metroplex math holds up too, at about 15 minutes to downtown Fort Worth, 17 to DFW Airport, and 22 to downtown Dallas, so the address trades nothing for its postcard streets. Homes turn over slowly here, which tells you most of what you need to know.
arlington/interlochen.homes: Expect established brick homes — one and two stories, many custom-built for their day — on lots sized for real backyards, the best of which run straight down to the canals. Waterfront addresses are the marquee inventory in Interlochen and rarely linger; interior streets deliver the same tree cover for less. Condition varies house to house, from thoughtfully renovated to time-capsule original, so plan on touring widely and budgeting honestly for updates. It suits buyers who would take setting and mature landscaping over new-build finishes — and who don't mind stringing a few thousand lights when December rolls around.

highlights.title: Holiday light tradition
highlights.note: December displays draw visitors from across DFW, with canal-front homes as the main stage.

highlights.title: Canal-front lots
highlights.note: Backyards step down to the water — a rarity anywhere in North Texas suburbia.

highlights.title: Mature tree canopy
highlights.note: Decades of growth shade streets in a way new subdivisions can't buy.

highlights.title: Slow-turnover streets
highlights.note: Long tenures and rare listings signal how residents feel about leaving.

faq.q: Why do people choose Interlochen?
faq.a: Residents tend to stay, which is the honest signal: the canals, the tree canopy, and the neighborly December ritual create the kind of attachment new subdivisions spend decades trying to earn. The trade-offs are older housing stock that may want updating and a December of steady visitor traffic — a small price, most here would tell you, and they'd know.

faq.q: What are the schools for Interlochen?
faq.a: Interlochen is served by Arlington ISD. As with any established neighborhood, campus assignments can change over time as the district adjusts boundaries, so verify the current elementary, junior high, and high school zoning for a specific address with Arlington ISD before making an offer. A listing agent can usually confirm, but the district's own map is the source of record.

faq.q: What are the Interlochen holiday lights?
faq.a: Every December, Interlochen residents light their homes and canal banks in a coordinated display that has become one of North Texas's best-known holiday traditions, drawing lines of slow-moving cars and plenty of on-foot admirers. If you buy here, consider participation semi-mandatory in the friendliest possible way — neighbors take the tradition seriously, and the collective effect is exactly why people visit.

faq.q: Do homes in Interlochen back to the canals?
faq.a: Some do, and those canal-front lots are the neighborhood's signature inventory — backyards stepping down to the water, often with decks or seating oriented toward it. Plenty of homes sit on interior streets without frontage, typically at friendlier prices, while sharing the same tree cover and December glow. Waterfront listings tend to move quickly whenever they surface, so be ready.

faq.q: Can you commute to Dallas or Fort Worth from Interlochen?
faq.a: The neighborhood sits near the middle of the metroplex's east-west axis: downtown Fort Worth is about 15 minutes, downtown Dallas about 22, and DFW Airport about 17. That positioning is part of why established Arlington neighborhoods keep their appeal — you're not choosing a downtown so much as keeping both of them within a reasonable drive.

arlington/southwest-arlington.tagline: Friday-night lights and long-tenure streets on Arlington's family side
intro: Southwest Arlington is where the city's family life concentrates: curving streets, two-car garages, basketball hoops at the curb, and a school calendar that organizes the whole year. The draw that agents lead with is zoning — much of this side of town feeds Arlington ISD's Martin High School pattern, and families plan their moves around it. The result is a steadiness you can feel driving through: kept yards, long tenures, weekend games.

It's also a practical place to run a household. The I-20 corridor puts groceries, big-box errands, and highway on-ramps close to most driveways, and the middle-of-the-metroplex position holds up — about 15 minutes to downtown Fort Worth, about 22 to downtown Dallas, about 17 to DFW Airport. What southwest Arlington doesn't offer is spectacle: no stadium fireworks, no sailing center. For the families who choose it, that's precisely the pitch.
arlington/southwest-arlington.homes: The stock is classic North Texas suburbia: brick one- and two-story homes on suburban lots, arranged along cul-de-sacs and gentle curves, with mature trees on the older streets and roomier floor plans toward the newer edges. Formal dining rooms, game rooms over the garage, covered patios — the family-house checklist is well represented here. Because the area built out over decades, condition and updates vary widely, which keeps options open across budgets. It suits buyers optimizing for space, schools, and stability over walkability or novelty — the household whose search starts with the Martin zone and works backward to the house.

highlights.title: Martin zone anchor
highlights.note: Much of the area feeds Arlington ISD's Martin High pattern — verify by address.

highlights.title: Cul-de-sac geometry
highlights.note: Courts and curves engineered for bikes, hoops, and slow traffic.

highlights.title: I-20 errand belt
highlights.note: Groceries, retail, and highway access sit a short drive from most streets.

highlights.title: Built-out steadiness
highlights.note: Established blocks, long tenures, and yards kept with visible pride.

faq.q: What is it like to live in Southwest Arlington?
faq.a: For families, it's one of the most straightforward yes answers in Arlington. The school zoning drives demand, the streets were built for kids, and the I-20 corridor handles the logistics. What it won't give you is nightlife or new-build gloss — this is established suburbia doing established-suburbia things. Buyers who want walkable restaurants or warranty-fresh construction usually land happier elsewhere in DFW.

faq.q: What are the schools for Southwest Arlington?
faq.a: Arlington ISD serves the area, and the Martin High School feeder pattern is the specific draw for many buyers on this side of the city. Zoning is set address by address, though, and boundaries can shift over time — confirm the current campus assignments for any home you're considering directly with Arlington ISD rather than trusting a listing description.

faq.q: Can you buy new construction in Southwest Arlington?
faq.a: Not many — this side of the city is largely built out, so new construction is limited to occasional infill or the odd teardown-rebuild. Buyers set on a brand-new home in Arlington generally look north to Viridian, where builders are actively selling. In the southwest, the play is established homes, with renovation potential doing the work new construction does elsewhere.

faq.q: How long is the drive to downtown Dallas or Fort Worth from Southwest Arlington?
faq.a: Downtown Fort Worth runs about 15 minutes and downtown Dallas about 22, with DFW Airport at about 17 — southwest Arlington keeps the city's split-the-difference geography. Direct I-20 access makes east-west commutes simpler than the map suggests, and even Legacy West in Plano is workable at about 42 minutes, though few here make that drive every day.

arlington/viridian.tagline: Sailboats, shoreline trails, and Arlington's boldest master-plan bet
intro: Viridian turned Arlington's north side into one of the most talked-about master plans in DFW, and it did it with water. Lakes anchor the layout, a community sailing center puts actual boats on them, and trail connections run toward River Legacy's shaded miles. Mornings look like paddleboards and stroller traffic; evenings look like neighbors making the shoreline loop before dinner. It's an unusual amount of scenery for landlocked North Texas.

The location does quiet work too. DFW Airport is about 17 minutes out, downtown Fort Worth about 15, and downtown Dallas about 22, which makes Viridian one of the rare new communities that splits the metroplex evenly instead of picking a side. Add active construction phases and a steady calendar of neighborhood events, and you get a place that still feels like it's becoming something — in a good way.
arlington/viridian.homes: Viridian is new-build territory: a roster of builders runs from cottage-scale lots to lake-facing showpieces, with current phases selling from the $420s. The architecture holds to a plan-wide standard — porches, varied rooflines, alley-loaded garages on some streets — which gives the sidewalks a consistency piecemeal subdivisions never manage. Lots run tighter than old-school Arlington, a trade most residents make gladly for water, parks, and trail access at the end of the block. It suits first-timers stretching into a new build, move-up families, and empty nesters who would rather sail than mow.

highlights.title: Lakes on tap
highlights.note: Open water threads the plan, with shoreline paths and gathering spots along the banks.

highlights.title: Community sailing center
highlights.note: Small craft and lessons put actual sailboats on Arlington water.

highlights.title: River Legacy links
highlights.note: Trail connections link straight into the wooded greenbelt corridor next door.

highlights.title: Now-selling phases
highlights.note: New construction from the $420s, with multiple builders releasing lots in stages.

faq.q: Who is Viridian right for?
faq.a: For buyers who want new construction with something to do outside, it's one of the strongest picks in North Texas. The lakes and sailing center give it an identity most master plans can't match, the trail network connects toward River Legacy, and the location splits Dallas and Fort Worth almost evenly. The trade-offs are ongoing construction and tighter lots than older Arlington neighborhoods.

faq.q: Can you buy new construction in Viridian?
faq.a: Yes — Viridian is actively selling, with new homes from the $420s across multiple builders and product lines. Phases release in stages, so available floor plans and lots shift through the year. Quick move-in inventory homes and build-from-dirt contracts are both typically on the table; which one makes sense depends on your timeline and your appetite for design decisions.

faq.q: What are the schools for Viridian?
faq.a: Arlington ISD is the district associated with the city, but school zoning in fast-growing master plans is set address by address and can shift as new campuses open. Before you contract on a specific lot, confirm the current campus assignments with the district. Builder sales offices keep zoning maps on hand — ask to see the latest one rather than relying on a listing.

faq.q: Can you commute to Dallas or Fort Worth from Viridian?
faq.a: Downtown Fort Worth runs about 15 minutes and downtown Dallas about 22, which puts Viridian close to the metroplex's geographic sweet spot. DFW Airport is about 17 minutes — a real perk for frequent flyers — and even Legacy West in Plano is reachable at about 42. Few communities let a two-career household split opposite downtowns this cleanly.

faq.q: What is inside Viridian?
faq.a: Water is the headline: community lakes thread through the neighborhood, and the sailing center puts residents on them with small craft and lessons. Trails loop the shorelines and connect toward River Legacy's wooded corridor, and parks and greens are scattered through the phases. It's an amenity set built around being outside rather than around a single clubhouse.

faq.q: How competitive is Viridian right now?
faq.a: Viridian's central-metro position keeps a steady buyer stream — the live MLS-matched count on this page tracks what's actually available. Entry runs from the $420s. Pricing and releases change quickly — verify current availability with the sales offices.

faq.q: What should I compare Viridian against?
faq.a: Walsh on Fort Worth's west side is the other big master plan flanking Tarrant County — more acreage-scaled, higher band. The Arlington guide on this site maps the established neighborhoods if new construction isn't a must.

amenities: Sailing center with lessons and small-craft launches
Trail links to the River Legacy corridor
Walking and biking loops throughout the phases
buyerNotes: With multiple builders selling at once, walk more than one model row before writing a contract — floor plans overlap in price but differ in standard features, and the base-price gap often narrows once you compare spec sheets side by side.

Water-facing and greenbelt-backing lots typically carry premiums and release in waves. If a view matters to you, get on the lot-release list early and ask which phases still hold inventory instead of settling for what's on today's map.

aubrey/old-town-aubrey.tagline: Where Aubrey's original streets still run on porch time
intro: Old Town Aubrey existed before the master plans arrived: an original street grid shaded by trees that have been at it far longer than the subdivisions down the road. Life here moves at porch speed: waves from pickups, kids cutting across familiar yards, downtown storefronts a short walk or an even shorter drive away. It's the small-town center that gives the rest of Aubrey its accent.

What makes Old Town interesting right now is the contrast. North Texas growth is closing in from every direction (the tollway extension, the 380 corridor, new rooftops on old pasture), yet these blocks keep their big trees and their unhurried habits. Living here means Friday-night football within earshot, feed stores that still know their customers, and a front-row seat to a town negotiating its next chapter. For DFW buyers tired of beige sameness, that's the draw.
aubrey/old-town-aubrey.homes: Housing in Old Town Aubrey is the opposite of a production lineup: frame cottages and bungalows from earlier eras, ranch-style homes with genuinely deep lots, and the occasional newer infill build slotted between longtime residents. Trees are mature, setbacks are generous, and no two blocks quite match. This is territory for buyers who'd rather renovate character than buy it new: handy owners, small-scale investors, and anyone who wants elbow room without leaving town. Inspect carefully — older homes reward diligence on foundations, plumbing, and roofs — and price the charm accordingly.

faq.q: Why do people choose Old Town Aubrey?

The trade-off is older housing stock that asks for maintenance and patience. For buyers who want a home with a backstory, that's a fair bargain.

faq.q: Which school district covers Old Town Aubrey?

Buyers set on brand-new construction usually look to Aubrey's master plans and newer communities nearby; buyers drawn to Old Town are typically shopping for exactly what those places can't offer — age, trees, and personality.

faq.q: How far is Old Town Aubrey from downtown Dallas or Fort Worth?
faq.a: Downtown Dallas is about 48 minutes and downtown Fort Worth about 58, with DFW Airport about 38 and Legacy West in Plano about 27. Numbers aside, part of Old Town's appeal is how rarely you need the long drives. Daily errands stay local, and the corridor retail along 380 fills most gaps.

aubrey/sandbrock-ranch.tagline: Ranch land roots, resort pool afternoons, west of town
intro: Sandbrock Ranch takes the west side of Aubrey and turns old ranch land into the kind of master plan people move across DFW for. The center of gravity is the resort-style pool in summer and the fishing lakes the rest of the year — water, big sky, and streets built for evening walks. An on-site elementary means the school run can be a bike ride, which changes the shape of a weekday morning more than any floor plan does.

The location works because Aubrey's west side is where new North Texas is arriving fastest. The Dallas North Tollway extension keeps shortening the drive south — Legacy West in Plano runs about 27 minutes, and DFW Airport about 38 — while the land immediately around the community still reads as horse country. You get feed-store Texas on the weekend errand and a real amenity calendar at home, which is a rarer combination than the marketing brochures make it sound.
aubrey/sandbrock-ranch.homes: New construction dominates here, with several builders selling side by side and pricing that starts from the $400s. Expect brick-and-stone elevations with modern-farmhouse touches, open family rooms, and covered back patios sized for a Texas evening. Lots range from tidy interior homesites to premium spots along the water, and the streetscapes feel planned rather than accidental — front porches and sidewalks that actually connect. It suits families chasing the on-site elementary, move-up buyers who want amenities without a country-club bill, and anyone betting early on the DNT corridor's next decade.

aubrey/silverado.tagline: Practical new rooftops where the tollway meets the prairie
intro: Silverado is Aubrey's straightforward answer to a straightforward question: where can a household still buy a new home in DFW without the payment swallowing the rest of life? The community sits off the Dallas North Tollway extension, which means the value proposition comes with a real commute story attached. Streets fill with strollers and pickup trucks in roughly equal measure, and neighbors tend to be at the same stage of building a life.

Daily rhythms here are simple in the best way. Legacy West in Plano is about 27 minutes down the tollway for the office crowd, DFW Airport about 38 for the road warriors, and the rest of Aubrey — Friday-night football, feed stores, the old downtown grid — is minutes in the other direction. Silverado buyers aren't paying for a lagoon; they're paying for a front door in North Texas's growth path, and that math keeps working.
aubrey/silverado.homes: The housing stock is newer single-family construction built for efficiency: open-concept main floors, upstairs game rooms on the two-story plans, and brick-front elevations that keep maintenance sane. Lots run compact, which trades yard work for weekend hours — a fair swap for plenty of buyers. Silverado suits first-time purchasers stretching into ownership, young families who want new systems and warranties instead of renovation projects, and investors watching the DNT extension pull value northward. If your priority list reads square footage, commute, and a garage that fits the truck, this corner of Aubrey deserves a tour.

You're close to the tollway when you need the metroplex and close to small-town Aubrey when you don't.

faq.q: Is anyone still building in Silverado?

faq.q: What school district serves Silverado?

aubrey/winn-ridge.tagline: Starter streets with a straight shot to the 380 corridor
intro: Winn Ridge is where a lot of Aubrey stories begin — the first mortgage, the first backyard, the first neighbor who becomes a friend because your kids claimed the same stretch of sidewalk. The community sits near US 380, which puts groceries, gyms, and the whole corridor's growing retail strip within a few easy minutes. It's an unpretentious neighborhood, and it wears that well.

Life near 380 means you feel North Texas growing in real time — new signals, new storefronts, new neighbors — but Winn Ridge itself stays residential and calm once you turn off the highway. Evenings are bikes in driveways and grills going on back patios. For commuters, Legacy West in Plano sits about 27 minutes out and DFW Airport about 38, close enough that living in Aubrey doesn't mean opting out of the metroplex.
aubrey/winn-ridge.homes: Expect approachable single-family homes on manageable lots — floor plans that put every dollar into livable space rather than grand gestures. Elevations mix brick and siding, layouts favor open kitchens and flexible secondary bedrooms, and backyards are sized for a swing set and a smoker, not a tractor. Winn Ridge fits first-time buyers graduating from apartments along the 380 corridor, young families planting a flag in Aubrey ISD territory, and downsizers who want newer construction without master-plan pricing. Entry-level rooftops near a growth corridor keep finding their audience, which is exactly what you want from a starter neighborhood.

faq.q: Which school district covers Winn Ridge?

faq.q: How far is Winn Ridge from downtown Dallas or Fort Worth?
faq.a: Figure about 48 minutes to downtown Dallas and about 58 to downtown Fort Worth. The more common drives are shorter: DFW Airport is about 38 minutes and Legacy West in Plano about 27, and being near US 380 gives you flexible routes east and west across the metroplex's northern edge.

faq.q: Can you buy new construction in Winn Ridge?
faq.a: Winn Ridge developed as a newer community, so the streets mix recent builds with early resales. Depending on timing you may find builder inventory nearby or a gently used home already finished with blinds, gutters, and a landscaped yard — often the better deal for a starter budget. A local agent can tell you what's active right now.

aurora/114-frontage.tagline: Frontage land betting patiently on the 114 corridor
intro: US 114 is Aurora's main artery, and the frontage tracts along it are where the town's quiet land game gets played. Owners out here tend to think in decades: hold the road-front acreage, run some cattle or cut some hay, and watch the metroplex's northwest edge work its way up the highway. With Texas Motor Speedway about fifteen minutes away and Fort Worth growing toward it, patience has a logic to it.

Day to day, 114 frontage living is more pastoral than the word 'frontage' suggests — most tracts hold a house set well back from the road, with the highway hum fading fast behind the first rise. You keep Northwest ISD schools, a straight shot of about 29 minutes to downtown Fort Worth, and about 34 to DFW Airport. It's rural Aurora living with an exit strategy built into the deed.
aurora/114-frontage.homes: Real estate along Aurora's 114 frontage is a land play wearing a homestead's clothes. Listings range from older ranch houses on large road-front tracts to raw parcels with nothing but fence and possibility. The house matters less than the dirt: buyers underwrite the acreage, the highway access, and the corridor's long-term direction, then treat the residence as a bonus or a project. It suits buyer-investors, small-business owners eyeing future visibility subject to city approvals, and families happy to live well on land that may be doing quiet work in the background. Bring patience and a good survey.

faq.q: Why do people choose 114 frontage in Aurora?
