The result feels more like a small lakeside district than a subdivision — morning runners, lunch crowds, happy hours that spill outside when North Texas weather cooperates.

Daily life runs on proximity. DFW Airport sits about 9 minutes away, downtown Dallas about 22, and Legacy West about 20 — numbers that make Cypress Waters a favorite for frequent flyers and dual-commute households. Evenings are patios and lakeside loops rather than backyard fences, and the crowd skews professional and social. If classic Coppell is porches and cul-de-sacs, this is its urban-leaning cousin on the water.
coppell/cypress-waters.homes: Residences at Cypress Waters run urban-format: lofts and apartment-style homes stacked near the offices and restaurants, built for people who want the district at their doorstep. For-sale inventory inside the development is limited — much of the housing is lease-based — so buyers drawn to the lakeside lifestyle often shop the established Coppell neighborhoods a few minutes away and keep Cypress Waters as their patio-and-trails amenity. It suits young professionals, airport-adjacent road warriors, and anyone easing into DFW who wants to try the area before committing to a yard.

highlights.title: Lakeside Trails
highlights.note: Paths trace the shoreline for morning runs and post-dinner walks.

highlights.title: Walk-to-Work Offices
highlights.note: Employer campuses share the district, shrinking some commutes to a stroll.

highlights.title: Patio Dining Row
highlights.note: Restaurants line the water, busiest when the weather plays nice.

highlights.title: Airport in Minutes
highlights.note: About 9 minutes to DFW Airport — catnip for frequent flyers.

faq.q: Why do people choose Cypress Waters?
faq.a: For a walkable, social, lake-adjacent routine, it's one of the more distinctive addresses in the DFW area. Offices, restaurants, and residences share the shoreline, so daily life needs less windshield time. It suits professionals and frequent travelers more than buyers hunting big yards — for those, classic Coppell neighborhoods nearby fill the gap.

faq.q: Which school district covers Cypress Waters?
faq.a: Coppell ISD is the district associated with the community, and its reputation carries real weight with families across North Texas. Because Cypress Waters sits at the edge of several boundary lines, verify the assigned campuses for any specific residence before you sign — district maps, not marketing materials, are the source of truth.

faq.q: Are there homes for sale in Cypress Waters?
faq.a: The residential stock leans heavily toward lofts and apartment-style leasing rather than traditional for-sale homes, so purchase opportunities inside the district are limited and worth watching closely when they surface. Many buyers who love the setting end up purchasing in nearby Coppell neighborhoods and treating Cypress Waters as their dining-and-trails backyard.

faq.q: How far is Cypress Waters from downtown Dallas or Fort Worth?
faq.a: Downtown Dallas is about 22 minutes and downtown Fort Worth about 29, with DFW Airport a standout at about 9 minutes. Legacy West in Plano comes in around 20 minutes. Few DFW addresses put both downtowns, the airport, and a lakeside patio scene inside a half-hour radius, which is a big part of the appeal.

faq.q: What is inside Cypress Waters?
faq.a: The lake is the centerpiece, ringed by trails, patios, and green gathering spaces, with restaurants and coffee stops built into the district's daily rhythm. Office campuses keep it lively on weekdays; evenings and weekends bring runners, dog walkers, and dinner crowds. It functions less like an amenity list and more like a small waterfront main street.

coppell/lakes-of-coppell.tagline: Ponds out back, cul-de-sacs out front, everything else nearby
intro: Lakes of Coppell earns its name honestly: ponds thread through the neighborhood, stitched together by greenbelt paths that turn an evening walk into a small nature tour. This is Coppell's family core — bikes in driveways, fishing lines off the banks, cul-de-sacs that host more games than the parks do. The water does something subtle to the streets, breaking up rooftops with open sky and giving plenty of homes a view.

Position is the other draw. Schools, parks, and everyday errands sit within a short drive, and the longer drives stay short: DFW Airport about 9 minutes, downtown Dallas about 22, Legacy West about 20. Weekends look like this: ballfields in the morning, the Coppell farmers market if you're quick, pond loops before dinner. It's the kind of neighborhood people describe by pointing at their kids.
coppell/lakes-of-coppell.homes: The housing stock is family-scaled brick traditional through and through: four-bedroom floor plans, game rooms, covered patios, and yards sized for trampolines. Pond-adjacent lots are the ones neighbors covet: water views and greenbelt access without leaving the block. Streets are mature, landscaping established, and the overall feel is a neighborhood built all of a piece rather than in scattered phases. Lakes of Coppell suits move-up families who want room to grow inside Coppell ISD's boundaries, and buyers who'd rather have proven schools and pond views than a brand-new kitchen — though plenty of resales arrive updated anyway.

highlights.title: Pond Network
highlights.note: Water threads the neighborhood, with greenbelt paths linking the banks.

highlights.title: Family Cul-de-sacs
highlights.note: Low-traffic streets where driveway basketball is practically the local sport.

highlights.title: Everything Close
highlights.note: Schools, parks, and errands sit minutes from the front door.

highlights.title: Evening Loop Walks
highlights.note: Pond-side paths make the after-dinner walk a neighborhood institution.

faq.q: Why do people choose Lakes of Coppell?
faq.a: For families it's about as on-the-nose as Coppell gets: ponds and greenbelt paths woven through quiet streets, kid-heavy cul-de-sacs, and the city's school-first culture in full effect. The trade-off is demand — homes here rarely linger, and choice is limited at any given moment. Most residents consider that a feature, not a bug.

faq.q: What school district serves Lakes of Coppell?
faq.a: Coppell ISD, and for many buyers that's the headline. Coppell is a town where the school district and the city identity are hard to separate, and Lakes of Coppell sits squarely in that culture. As always in North Texas, double-check campus assignments for a specific address, since boundaries are set by the district.

faq.q: Do homes in Lakes of Coppell have water views?
faq.a: A good number do. Ponds lace through the neighborhood, so lots backing or siding to water come up regularly compared with most DFW subdivisions — though they're still the first listings to draw crowds. If a view is non-negotiable, tell your agent early and be ready to act when the right lot surfaces.

faq.q: Is anyone still building in Lakes of Coppell?
faq.a: No — this is an established, built-out neighborhood, and Coppell overall has very little raw land left, which is exactly why its resale market stays tight. Buyers wanting new construction typically look to communities farther out in the metroplex; buyers wanting Lakes of Coppell accept resale and often renovate to taste over time.

faq.q: How far is Lakes of Coppell from downtown Dallas or DFW Airport?
faq.a: DFW Airport is the showstopper at about 9 minutes; downtown Dallas runs about 22 and downtown Fort Worth about 29. Legacy West in Plano is about 20 minutes for north-corridor commuters. Ponds at home and every major job center within half an hour: that's why families dig in here.

coppell/old-town-coppell.tagline: Market mornings and porch-swing evenings on Coppell's original streets
intro: Saturday in Old Town Coppell starts early: growers setting up stalls at the farmers market, coffee moving down Main Street, neighbors trading tomatoes and gossip in roughly equal measure. This is the part of Coppell that carries the town's brand — small-scale, porch-forward, built for lingering. In a suburb boxed in by DFW Airport and three highways, Old Town is the spot where the pace drops to a walk.

Living here means the market, the square, and a handful of restaurants sit within strolling distance, while the rest of North Texas stays close: the airport is about 9 minutes away and downtown Dallas about 22. Community events fill the calendar — market Saturdays, seasonal festivals on the green — and the cottage streets keep things neighborly by design. It's small-town Texas with a very connected zip code.
coppell/old-town-coppell.homes: Housing in Old Town Coppell leans cottage: porch-fronted homes with bungalow proportions, tidy lots, and detailing that nods to the town's early streets. Some are newer builds designed to match the historic scale; others are originals that have been loved on for decades. Yards are modest, which is the point — the front porch does the entertaining. It suits downsizers who want to walk to the market, first-time buyers chasing character over square footage, and anyone in DFW who'd rather know their neighbors than their commute playlist. Inventory is thin and turnover slow, so serious buyers should be ready to move.

highlights.title: Farmers Market Saturdays
highlights.note: The weekly market anchors the neighborhood's social calendar, rain or shine.

highlights.title: Cottage Streetscape
highlights.note: Porch-forward homes at a walkable scale you rarely find in newer DFW suburbs.

highlights.title: Main Street Strolls
highlights.note: Coffee, patios, and small shops within a few unhurried blocks.

highlights.title: Airport-Close Calm
highlights.note: About 9 minutes to DFW Airport without feeling like you live at one.

faq.q: Why do people choose Old Town Coppell?
faq.a: If walkability and community texture rank high on your list, yes. Old Town concentrates Coppell's farmers market, events, and restaurant patios into a few strollable blocks, and the cottage streets keep the scale human. The trade-off is limited inventory and smaller lots — this is a neighborhood you choose for lifestyle first, square footage second.

faq.q: What school district serves Old Town Coppell?
faq.a: Coppell ISD serves the city, and the district's reputation is a big part of why families plant roots here and stay. As with any North Texas address, confirm the assigned campuses for a specific home before you write an offer — attendance boundaries can shift as the district plans for growth.

faq.q: What kinds of homes are for sale in Old Town Coppell?
faq.a: Expect cottage-style homes with front porches, compact yards, and architecture scaled to the historic streets — some newer construction built to match, some longtime originals. Listings are infrequent and tend to draw attention quickly, so buyers who want in should set alerts and be ready to tour the same week a home hits the market.

faq.q: How far is Old Town Coppell from downtown Dallas or Fort Worth?
faq.a: Downtown Dallas runs about 22 minutes, downtown Fort Worth about 29, and DFW Airport is about 9 minutes away. Legacy West in Plano is about 20 minutes. That mid-metroplex position is a quiet superpower: Old Town feels tucked away, but almost every major DFW job center sits within a short drive.

faq.q: What is the Coppell Farmers Market like?
faq.a: It's the neighborhood's front porch: local growers, makers, and a steady crowd of regulars filling the market grounds on Saturdays. For Old Town residents it doubles as a weekly social hour — you'll run into neighbors, teachers, and half your street. Even Coppell folks from other neighborhoods treat it as the town's gathering spot.

coppell/riverchase.tagline: Golf-course mornings on Coppell's most established loop
intro: Riverchase organizes itself around two things: a golf course and a loop. Homes line the fairways and the parkway that circles them, so the neighborhood reads green from almost any driveway — mature trees, open turf, the occasional errant tee shot. It's the kind of established Coppell address where the landscaping has had time to settle in and the neighbors measure tenure in graduations, not lease terms.

Life here is unhurried in a way that belies the location. DFW Airport is about 9 minutes out, downtown Dallas about 22, and downtown Fort Worth about 29 — yet inside the loop it's golf carts, dog walkers, and porch flags. Everyday Coppell errands stay close, and the neighborhood's North Texas practicality shows in how little turnover the streets see. People arrive for the schools and stay for the scenery.
coppell/riverchase.homes: Riverchase homes are the classic North Texas playbook done well: brick traditionals, formal-and-family floor plans, two-car garages, and lawns that have clearly been someone's weekend hobby. Fairway-backing lots are the neighborhood's trophy addresses, with views of turf and trees instead of a rear fence. Lot sizes feel generous by modern standards, and the mature canopy does a lot of the curb-appeal work. It suits families who want established over shiny, golfers who like their course commute measured in steps, and buyers seeking a resale home with room to update on their own timeline.

highlights.title: Fairway Frontage
highlights.note: Golf-course lots trade back fences for long green views.

highlights.title: The Loop
highlights.note: A circling parkway gives the whole neighborhood its walking route.

highlights.title: Mature Canopy
highlights.note: Established trees shade streets that newer subdivisions can't replicate yet.

highlights.title: Nine Minutes to DFW
highlights.note: About 9 minutes to the airport makes travel days painless.

faq.q: What is it like to live in Riverchase?
faq.a: It's one of Coppell's steadiest bets: an established golf-course neighborhood where homes hold their appeal, streets stay quiet, and the loop gives everyone a built-in walking route. Buyers who want brand-new finishes should look elsewhere, but if mature trees and settled streets sound better than construction dust, Riverchase makes a strong case.

faq.q: Which school district covers Riverchase?
faq.a: Coppell ISD is the district named for the city, and its reputation is a major reason families shop here in the first place. School attendance boundaries in this corner of Dallas County can be particular, though, so confirm the assigned campuses for any specific Riverchase address with the district before making an offer.

faq.q: Do homes in Riverchase back up to the golf course?
faq.a: Many do — fairway-backing lots are the neighborhood's signature, trading a standard rear fence for open green views. They command a premium and don't surface often, so if a course lot is the goal, patience and a fast pre-approval help. Interior-street homes still get the loop, the trees, and the same quiet.

faq.q: Are there new construction homes in Riverchase?
faq.a: Riverchase is an established, built-out neighborhood, so new construction is rare — what you'll find instead is a steady trickle of resales, some lovingly updated and some priced as projects. In land-scarce Coppell, teardown-and-rebuild activity occasionally happens in mature areas, but buyers should come expecting resale inventory, not model homes.

faq.q: What are commutes like from Riverchase?
faq.a: Plan on about 22 minutes to downtown Dallas and about 29 to downtown Fort Worth, with DFW Airport just about 9 minutes away and Legacy West in Plano about 20. For a neighborhood that feels this settled, the reach across the metroplex is remarkable — one reason Riverchase households tend to stay put.

dallas/bishop-arts.tagline: Where Oak Cliff keeps its porches and its record shops
intro: Bishop Arts works on foot, which still makes it an outlier in Dallas. The district itself is a compact grid of local shops — pie counters, taquerias, bookstores, bars with actual regulars — and the blocks around it are old Oak Cliff: craftsman bungalows, wide porches, neighbors who wave. Living here means walking to dinner most nights and knowing the person who pours your coffee by name.

The setting is North Oak Cliff, across the Trinity from downtown, and the skyline view from this side of the river is the best in the city. The streetcar links the district toward downtown Dallas, and the drive is about 8 minutes when you'd rather not wait. It's a neighborhood in motion — restoration next to renovation next to the house that hasn't changed since Eisenhower — and that mix is exactly the appeal.
dallas/bishop-arts.homes: Housing around Bishop Arts is classic Oak Cliff stock: craftsman bungalows with deep porches, tidy cottages, and foursquares on compact, walkable lots. Renovation quality varies house to house — some are down-to-the-studs restorations, others honest fixer projects — and townhomes and small condo buildings have filled in along the district's edges. It suits buyers who'd trade a big suburban yard for a five-minute walk to dinner: first-time owners, design-minded renovators, and anyone in North Texas who wants urban living at bungalow scale instead of high-rise scale.

highlights.title: Walkable District
highlights.note: Shops, taquerias, galleries, and bars packed into a few genuinely strollable blocks.

highlights.title: Dallas Streetcar
highlights.note: A rail link pointing the neighborhood toward downtown Dallas without the parking hassle.

highlights.title: Skyline Views
highlights.note: The Trinity-side angle on the Dallas skyline is the city's best postcard.

highlights.title: Bungalow Blocks
highlights.note: Craftsman porches and mature trees within walking distance of the storefronts.

faq.q: What is it like to live in Bishop Arts?
faq.a: It's one of the few Dallas neighborhoods where you can genuinely live on foot, and the community is tight in the way old streetcar neighborhoods tend to be. Weekends bring visitors and parking pressure to the district blocks, so many residents prefer being a few streets removed — close enough to walk, far enough to sleep.

faq.q: What are the schools for Bishop Arts?
faq.a: Bishop Arts and the surrounding North Oak Cliff blocks are served by Dallas ISD. As anywhere in a big urban district, school boundaries vary street by street, so verify the assigned campuses for any specific address and tour them — several nearby schools have strong neighborhood followings.

faq.q: Can you commute to Dallas or Fort Worth from Bishop Arts?
faq.a: Downtown Dallas sits just across the Trinity River — about 8 minutes by car, or a streetcar ride if you'd rather skip parking. Downtown Fort Worth is about 33 minutes, DFW Airport about 20, and Legacy West in Plano about 25. For an urban neighborhood, the commute math is friendly.

faq.q: Are there new construction homes in Bishop Arts?
faq.a: Not in the master-planned sense — this is an established neighborhood. New construction here mostly means townhomes and small infill projects near the district, plus custom rebuilds scattered through the bungalow blocks. Buyers wanting brand-new should watch infill listings closely; they move fast in walkable pockets like this one.

faq.q: Is Bishop Arts competitive for buyers?
faq.a: Yes — walkable Dallas neighborhoods with this much character are scarce, and renovated bungalows draw multiple offers in most seasons. Patience and a pre-approval letter matter more here than almost anywhere in Oak Cliff.

faq.q: What should I compare Bishop Arts against?
faq.a: Lakewood offers the other flavor of storied Dallas — lake trails instead of retail strips. The Dallas guide on this site maps both alongside Preston Hollow and the rest of the city's marquee neighborhoods.

seo.title: Bishop Arts District, Dallas — Homes in Oak Cliff's Core
seo.description: Bishop Arts is Oak Cliff's walkable heart — bungalows and townhomes around Dallas's indie retail strip, minutes over the bridge from downtown.

dallas/lakewood.tagline: Storybook Tudors, lake mornings, and a canopy of old oaks
intro: Lakewood is the part of Dallas where the lake sets the schedule. Mornings mean runners and cyclists looping White Rock, kayaks on the water by eight, and coffee afterward in the Lakewood shopping district. The streets curve instead of grid, the oaks meet overhead, and the architecture — those famous Tudors the neighborhood is known for — gives every block a storybook profile you don't find in newer North Texas suburbs.

Day to day, it lives like a small town stitched into the city. Neighbors trade tomatoes and contractor recommendations, kids bike to the lake, and the Arboretum sits just down the shoreline for weekend wandering. Downtown Dallas is close enough — about 8 minutes on a good morning — that plenty of residents work in the towers and still make it home for a spillway sunset.
dallas/lakewood.homes: The signature stock is the 1930s Tudor — steep gables, arched doorways, brick and half-timber detail — set on generous lots under mature trees. Alongside them you'll find sprawling ranches, thoughtful renovations, and the occasional new custom home slipped onto an old footprint. Lots tend to be deeper than the Dallas norm, and the curvy streets near the lake carry some real elevation change. Lakewood suits buyers who want character over square-footage math: people willing to maintain an older home in exchange for architecture, canopy, and a front-row seat to White Rock Lake.

highlights.title: White Rock Lake
highlights.note: Miles of shoreline trail for running, cycling, and sailing, right at the neighborhood's edge.

highlights.title: Tudor Architecture
highlights.note: Steep gables and arched doors give Lakewood blocks a storybook profile.

highlights.title: Lakewood Shopping District
highlights.note: Restaurants, coffee, and the old theater marquee anchor the neighborhood's main crossing.

highlights.title: Dallas Arboretum Nearby
highlights.note: Seasonal gardens along the lake's southeast shore, an easy weekend default.

faq.q: What is it like to live in Lakewood?
faq.a: If you want an established Dallas neighborhood with real architecture and daily access to green space, Lakewood is hard to beat. The trade-offs are the ones that come with older homes — maintenance, quirks, the occasional foundation conversation — but residents tend to stay put for decades, which tells you most of what you need to know.

faq.q: What are the schools for Lakewood?
faq.a: Lakewood is served by Dallas ISD. Families here also weigh a range of private and charter options around East Dallas, so it's worth touring campuses and confirming campus assignments for any specific address, since boundaries can shift over time.

faq.q: Can you commute to Dallas or Fort Worth from Lakewood?
faq.a: Downtown Dallas is about 8 minutes away, which is part of the neighborhood's whole pitch: lake life on one side, skyline on the other. Downtown Fort Worth runs about 33 minutes, DFW Airport about 20, and the Legacy West job cluster in Plano about 25 — all manageable from the east side.

faq.q: Are there new construction homes in Lakewood?
faq.a: Lakewood is an established neighborhood, so there are no large new-build communities here. New construction shows up as individual custom homes and rebuilds on existing lots. If you want new-home warranties and design centers, look to DFW's master-planned suburbs; if you want Lakewood, plan on older stock or a custom project.

faq.q: What is there to do near Lakewood?
faq.a: White Rock Lake is the anchor — trails, sailing, birding, the spillway. The Dallas Arboretum sits on the lake's southeast shore, and the Lakewood shopping district covers dinner, coffee, and a movie. Lower Greenville and East Dallas's restaurant rows are minutes away when you want a bigger night out.

faq.q: Is Lakewood competitive for buyers?
faq.a: Consistently — Lakewood households tend to stay, so listings are scarce relative to demand and well-priced homes near the lake move quickly. Watch for estate sales and original-condition listings if you want a renovation entry point.

faq.q: What should I compare Lakewood against?
faq.a: Preston Hollow for lot size and quiet money; Bishop Arts for walkability over lake access. The Dallas guide on this site puts the three side by side with the rest of the city.

seo.title: Lakewood, Dallas TX — Homes Near White Rock Lake
seo.description: Lakewood runs from White Rock Lake to Lakewood Shopping Center — storied Dallas architecture, lake trails, and a fiercely loyal resale market.

dallas/m-streets.tagline: Steep gables, shady blocks, Greenville Avenue at the corner
intro: The M Streets earned their nickname honestly — Monticello, Mercedes, McCommas and their neighbors run in a tight, leafy grid just off Greenville Avenue. The houses are the draw: gabled brick cottages with arched entries and chimneys doing a little architectural showing off. It's the kind of Dallas neighborhood where an evening walk turns into three sidewalk conversations and you get home after dark.

Lower Greenville sits at the neighborhood's doorstep, which means restaurants, live music, and a grocery run all happen without getting on a highway. Downtown Dallas is about 8 minutes when you do. The residents skew mixed in the best way — young couples on their first mortgage, families who upsized within the same three blocks, longtimers who remember every restaurant Greenville Avenue has ever hosted.
dallas/m-streets.homes: The M Streets are best known for Tudor-style cottages — steep rooflines, decorative brickwork, arched doors — shoulder to shoulder on walkable blocks, with Craftsman and revival styles mixed in. Lots are modest but the canopy is not; the trees here have had generations to fill in. Many homes have been expanded upward or back, so square footage varies more than the street view suggests. It suits buyers who want character and location over closet count — and who'd rather walk to brunch on Greenville than drive a loop of North Texas strip centers.

highlights.title: Lower Greenville
highlights.note: Restaurants, patios, and live music a short walk from most front doors.

highlights.title: Tudor Cottages
highlights.note: Steep rooflines and arched entries repeated block after photogenic block.

highlights.title: Walkable Grid
highlights.note: Sidewalks, alleys, and short blocks that make evening strolls the default.

highlights.title: Central Location
highlights.note: Minutes to downtown Dallas, White Rock Lake, and the Knox-Henderson corridor.

faq.q: Are the M Streets a good place to live?
faq.a: Yes, if walkable charm outranks square footage on your list. The M Streets pair architecture people cross the city to photograph with a bar-and-restaurant strip you can stroll to. The flip side: smaller lots, street parking on some blocks, and weekend noise near Greenville. Most residents consider that a fair trade.

faq.q: What school district serves the M Streets?
faq.a: The M Streets fall within Dallas ISD. Buyers here typically confirm the assigned campuses for a specific address early in the search, since zone lines in central Dallas can run down the middle of a neighborhood, and several nearby schools draw committed parent communities.

faq.q: How far are the M Streets from downtown Dallas or Fort Worth?
faq.a: Downtown Dallas runs about 8 minutes, straight down Central or surface streets when the highway argues. Downtown Fort Worth is about 33 minutes, DFW Airport about 20, and Legacy West in Plano about 25 — a central starting point for reaching anywhere in the metroplex.

faq.q: Are there new construction homes in the M Streets?
faq.a: Rarely as whole houses — conservation-minded neighbors and the value of original architecture keep most of the old stock standing. New construction here usually means substantial additions or the occasional rebuild. If a brand-new home is the priority, DFW's suburbs will serve you better; the M Streets sell character first.

dallas/preston-hollow.tagline: Deep lots, tall trees, and quiet money inside the loop
intro: Preston Hollow is where Dallas keeps its elbow room. The lots run wide and deep, the streets are quiet enough to hear sprinklers, and hedges do the work fences do elsewhere. It has long been the neighborhood of choice for people who could live anywhere in North Texas and chose to stay inside the city — close to offices, private schools, and every good restaurant north of downtown.

Daily life is easier than the gates suggest. Preston Center and NorthPark handle errands and retail, the Dallas North Tollway moves you north or south fast, and downtown Dallas is about 8 minutes on a clear morning. What you give up in walkability you get back in privacy: this is a neighborhood built around long driveways, backyard dinners, and the assumption that home is the destination.
dallas/preston-hollow.homes: Preston Hollow's housing runs from single-story ranch homes on generous lots to full estate compounds behind hedges and gates, with new custom construction steadily replacing older stock on the most coveted streets. Architecture is a survey course: traditional brick, Mediterranean, contemporary boxes with courtyards, because most of it was built one commission at a time. Lot size is the constant; privacy is the shared amenity. It suits buyers at the top of a Dallas search who want land and privacy without leaving the city, and patient ones who understand that in this neighborhood, the lot is often the real purchase.

highlights.title: Estate-Scale Lots
highlights.note: Wide, deep parcels with mature trees — rare land inside the Dallas city limits.

highlights.title: Preston Center Retail
highlights.note: Errands, lunches, and boutiques a short drive from home.

highlights.title: NorthPark Nearby
highlights.note: One of the country's best-known shopping centers sits minutes east.

highlights.title: Central Position
highlights.note: Tollway access puts downtown Dallas, the airport, and North Texas suburbs in easy reach.

faq.q: Is Preston Hollow a good place to live?
faq.a: For buyers who prize land, privacy, and a central Dallas address, few neighborhoods compete. It's quiet without being remote — Preston Center, NorthPark, and the Tollway are all minutes away. The lifestyle is car-based and home-centered, so if you want walkable nightlife, look east; if you want room, this is it.

faq.q: What are the schools for Preston Hollow?
faq.a: Preston Hollow is served by Dallas ISD, and the area is also home to several of the city's best-known private schools, which is part of the neighborhood's draw for many families. As always, confirm the assigned public campuses for a specific address before making school-driven decisions.

faq.q: How long is the drive to downtown Dallas or Fort Worth from Preston Hollow?
faq.a: Downtown Dallas is about 8 minutes via the Tollway or Central, which is remarkable given how far from urban the streets feel. DFW Airport runs about 20 minutes, Legacy West in Plano about 25, and downtown Fort Worth about 33. Useful numbers for two-career households pointed in different directions.

faq.q: Are there new construction homes in Preston Hollow?
faq.a: Yes, but not in subdivisions. New construction in Preston Hollow is custom work — an older ranch comes down, an architect-designed home goes up on the same lot. Buyers wanting new here either purchase a finished spec home or buy the lot and build. Either way, expect a longer timeline than a suburban new-build community.

decatur/fm-51-south.tagline: Fence lines to the horizon and a horse at the gate
intro: South of Decatur, FM 51 settles into a rhythm of pipe fencing, pasture, and mailboxes spaced like they're social distancing. This is the horse side of town — gooseneck trailers in the drive, arenas out back, hay delivered by the trailer-load — where property lines run long and the workday starts with feeding before coffee. If your real-estate search includes the word 'barn,' this stretch of North Texas is speaking your language.

For all the elbow room, town stays convenient: FM 51 runs straight into Decatur for the square, the vet, and everything a county seat keeps in stock, and Decatur ISD handles school days. Commuters point down US-287 — downtown Fort Worth is about 38 minutes from town — while DFW Airport comes in at about 48. It's a life with chores in it, and the people who choose it wouldn't trade.
decatur/fm-51-south.homes: Listings along FM 51 south lean horse property: single-story ranch houses and custom homes set back on acreage, with barns, loafing sheds, cross-fenced pasture, and the occasional lighted arena doing the heavy lifting in the photos. The land is the asset, so evaluate it like one — soil, grass, drainage, fencing condition, and water for both house and stock. Wells and septic are part of the deal on many parcels. It suits riders, ropers, breeders, and anybody who wants their horses at home instead of boarded — with Decatur's square just up the road when errands call.

highlights.title: Horse-ready parcels
highlights.note: Barns, arenas, and cross-fenced pasture show up in listings here as standard vocabulary.

highlights.title: Long fence lines
highlights.note: Pipe and wire run to the horizon; neighbors are a wave, not a wall.

highlights.title: Straight shot to town
highlights.note: FM 51 puts Decatur's square and services a few easy minutes north.

highlights.title: Trailer-friendly living
highlights.note: Room to turn a gooseneck around without a three-point plan and an audience.

faq.q: Is FM 51 south a good place to live?
faq.a: For horse people and land-first buyers, it's one of Decatur's best answers. You get acreage, quiet, and outbuildings that earn their keep, with town close enough that errands don't become expeditions. The tradeoffs are honest ones — well and septic maintenance, gravel dust, chores in August heat — and the people who live out here consider them a fair price.

faq.q: Can I keep horses on property along FM 51 south of Decatur?
faq.a: That's the neighborhood's calling card. Much of the land south of Decatur along FM 51 is set up for horses already — fencing, barns, pasture — though carrying capacity depends on the parcel's grass and water. Verify deed restrictions and current land use before closing, and walk the fence lines yourself; a listing photo never shows the sagging stretch.

faq.q: Which school district covers FM 51 south?
faq.a: Decatur ISD serves the Decatur side of the FM 51 corridor. Because rural boundaries in Wise County can change from one parcel to the next, confirm the district line and campus assignments for your specific property before you write a contract — your agent or the district office can pin it down quickly.

faq.q: How far is FM 51 south from Fort Worth or Dallas?
faq.a: From Decatur, downtown Fort Worth is about 38 minutes and downtown Dallas about 62, with DFW Airport at about 48 and Legacy West in Plano about 56. Properties farther down FM 51 add a few minutes of farm road first. Plenty of residents commute daily and consider the drive part of the decompression.

faq.q: What should I look for when buying horse property near Decatur?
faq.a: Water first: confirm the well or co-op service can cover troughs, wash racks, and the house. Then inspect fencing, barn structure and ventilation, pasture condition, drainage, and trailer access from the road. Review any deed restrictions on animals or arenas, and check floodplain maps. A rural-savvy inspector and lender make the whole process smoother.

decatur/greenwood-corridor.tagline: Where Decatur's pavement runs out and the pastures take over
intro: Head north out of Decatur toward Greenwood and town lets go of you fast — the streetlights quit, the fences start, and pretty soon the properties are measured in acres and the traffic is somebody's hay trailer. This is the corridor for buyers who mean it about country living: gravel drives, stock tanks, a shop building big enough for real projects, and lake water not far up the road.

Days out here run slower than anything the metroplex offers, but you're not off the grid. Decatur's square handles groceries, coffee, and the county business, US-287 picks up the commute (downtown Fort Worth runs about 38 minutes from town), and Decatur ISD covers the school run. It's the North Texas arrangement acreage buyers keep hunting for: genuine country on weeknights, a working town a short drive back down the road.
decatur/greenwood-corridor.homes: Real estate along the Greenwood corridor is acreage first, house second: ranch-style homes, custom builds, and farmhouses in every state of update, usually paired with barns, cross-fencing, and the metal shop that North Texas land buyers consider standard equipment. Wells and septic systems are common out here, so due diligence means water tests and system inspections, not just a foundation check. It suits horse people, hobby farmers, and anyone whose retirement plan involves a tractor — buyers who want land that works, with Decatur close enough for parts and biscuits.

highlights.title: Acreage that works
highlights.note: Land with room for barns, gardens, livestock, and at least one ambitious project.

highlights.title: Lake up the road
highlights.note: Water is north of here; weekend plans get a lot less complicated.

highlights.title: Dark-sky evenings
highlights.note: Far enough from town glow that the stars still put on a show.

highlights.title: Town within reach
highlights.note: Decatur's square covers groceries, coffee, and courthouse errands a short drive south.

faq.q: What is it like to live in the Greenwood corridor?
faq.a: If your idea of a good evening involves a tailgate, a pasture, and no neighbors in earshot, it's excellent. The corridor trades sidewalks and quick conveniences for acreage, quiet, and sky, with Decatur's square close enough for everything a small town covers. Buyers who want turnkey suburban ease should look in town; buyers who want land rarely regret it here.

faq.q: What are the schools for the Greenwood corridor?
faq.a: Decatur ISD serves the Decatur side of this corridor. Out in rural Wise County, district lines can shift road by road, so confirm the boundary and assigned campuses for any specific parcel with the district before you commit. The school run pairs with the feed-store run more often than not out here.

faq.q: Can I keep horses or livestock on land in the Greenwood corridor?
faq.a: Generally, yes. That's much of the point of buying north of Decatur. Most acreage out here supports horses, cattle, or a small flock, but always verify deed restrictions, current agricultural use, and fencing condition before closing. Water access matters too: confirm the well or co-op service can handle troughs as well as the house.

faq.q: How far is the Greenwood corridor from Fort Worth?
faq.a: From Decatur, downtown Fort Worth runs about 38 minutes down US-287, and you'll add your own drive in from the property. DFW Airport sits about 48 minutes out and downtown Dallas about 62. Plenty of corridor residents make the commute daily — it buys a workweek in the metroplex and every evening in the country.

faq.q: What should I check before buying acreage near Greenwood?
faq.a: The unglamorous stuff decides whether country life is fun: well output and water quality, septic condition and permits, easements and road frontage, floodplain mapping, fence lines versus survey lines, and any deed restrictions on animals or extra structures. Line up a lender familiar with rural and acreage purchases too — they underwrite differently than a tract-home loan.

decatur/sunset-ridge.tagline: Decatur's newest streets, one mile from its oldest square
intro: Sunset Ridge is where Decatur is growing — new streets on the west side where slabs get poured, frames go up, and the neighbors are all figuring out their sprinkler systems together. Models are open, three builders are at work, and the whole thing sits about a mile from the pink granite courthouse, which means your brand-new kitchen comes with a genuine county-seat square attached.

Living here is the easy version of small-town North Texas: house systems under warranty, Decatur ISD schools in the same town as your mailbox, and US-287 close by when work calls. Downtown Fort Worth is about 38 minutes, DFW Airport about 48 — near enough for the commute, far enough that Friday nights still belong to Decatur. For buyers who want new construction without a big-metro address, this is the reasonable answer.
decatur/sunset-ridge.homes: This is new-build territory, priced from the $340s, with three builders offering single-family plans across active phases. Expect the modern package — open kitchen-living layouts, primary suites that actually fit a king bed, energy-tight construction — on fresh streets where every roofline is still under warranty. Lots and elevations vary by phase, so walk the ground before you fall for a floor plan. Sunset Ridge suits first-time buyers, relocators, and anyone who likes the idea of choosing their own countertops a mile from Decatur's square.

highlights.title: Models open now
highlights.note: Finished model homes are touring; walk real plans instead of squinting at renderings.

highlights.title: Mile to the square
highlights.note: Coffee and biscuits by the courthouse are minutes away, not a highway project.

highlights.title: From the $340s
highlights.note: New-construction pricing that still leaves room in the budget for a back porch.

highlights.title: Decatur ISD
highlights.note: One town, one district — school spirit and street address match.

faq.q: Are there new construction homes in Sunset Ridge?
faq.a: Yes — Sunset Ridge is Decatur's active new-construction neighborhood, with three builders working, models open for touring, and homes priced from the $340s. Inventory shifts as phases release and close out, so check current availability with the builders directly. If you want a brand-new house inside Decatur proper rather than out on acreage, this is where to look.

faq.q: Is Sunset Ridge a good place to live in Decatur?
faq.a: It's a strong fit if you want new construction with a small-town backdrop. You get warrantied systems and modern layouts, plus the courthouse square about a mile away for coffee, errands, and Friday nights. The tradeoff is the usual new-neighborhood reality — young trees and construction traffic while phases build out — but that passes, and the town around it is already finished.

faq.q: Which school district covers Sunset Ridge?
faq.a: Sunset Ridge is served by Decatur ISD, the hometown district for the west side and the rest of town. Campus assignments vary by address, so verify the specific schools for your lot with the district before contract. Living and schooling in the same small town is a big part of the neighborhood's appeal.

faq.q: How far is Sunset Ridge from Fort Worth or DFW Airport?
faq.a: Plan on about 38 minutes to downtown Fort Worth and about 48 to DFW Airport, with US-287 doing most of the work. Downtown Dallas runs about 62 minutes and Legacy West in Plano about 56. It's a real commute, but a manageable one — and you come home to a new house in a courthouse-square town instead of a toll-tag suburb.

faq.q: What is inside Sunset Ridge?
faq.a: Sunset Ridge is a young community, so the headline features are the practical ones: new homes from three builders, model homes open for touring, fresh streets and sidewalks, and a location about a mile from Decatur's courthouse square. The town itself is the amenity package — coffee, boots, biscuits, and Friday night football, all a short drive from your driveway.

faq.q: How competitive is Sunset Ridge right now?
faq.a: Decatur's new-construction market is small and steady rather than frenzied — Sunset Ridge's $340s band faces little local competition. Pricing and releases change quickly — verify current availability with the sales offices.

faq.q: What should I compare Sunset Ridge against?
faq.a: Shale Creek in Rhome is the nearest new-build alternative down 287. If land is the real goal, the Greenwood corridor north of Decatur — covered in the Decatur guide on this site — is where the acreage starts.

amenities: One mile from the courthouse square
Quick access to US-287 and US-380
New streets and sidewalks on the west side
buyerNotes: Phase timing matters: early releases usually offer the best lot pick, while later phases mean finished streets and fewer nail guns at breakfast. Ask each builder for its release schedule and realistic completion dates before you commit earnest money.

Budget the design center before you visit it. Upgrades on flooring, cabinets, and electrical add up fast, and corner or oversized lots typically carry premiums. Decide your ceiling in advance and get the final feature list in writing.

Even with a builder warranty, pay for independent inspections at pre-drywall and before closing — new homes have punch lists too. Read the community's covenants and any HOA documents early, so fence styles and RV-parking rules don't surprise you later.

seo.title: Sunset Ridge — New Construction in Decatur From the $340s
seo.description: Sunset Ridge puts models-open new homes on Decatur's edge from the $340s — small-town square living with US-287 running the Fort Worth commute.

decatur/the-square-district.tagline: Victorian porches within earshot of the courthouse clock
intro: Life in the Square district orbits the pink granite courthouse the way the rest of Wise County does — except here, you can see it from the porch. These are Decatur's oldest blocks, where sidewalks buckle politely over pecan roots and the walk to coffee takes a few minutes, most of it spent waving at people. It's the rare North Texas address where 'running to the square' means putting on shoes, not starting the truck.

Day to day, it's a neighborhood that still behaves like one. Kids bike the grid, neighbors know whose Victorian got the new paint job, and when Decatur celebrates something on the square, you're already in the front row. Commuters aren't stranded either — US-287 is close, downtown Fort Worth runs about 38 minutes, and DFW Airport about 48, which keeps this old-town address surprisingly practical.
decatur/the-square-district.homes: Housing here is the real thing: Victorians with gingerbread trim and wraparound porches, joined over the decades by craftsman bungalows and tidy cottages, all on established blocks with trees that predate air conditioning. Condition varies house to house — some are lovingly restored, some are waiting on the right owner with a contractor's number — so a sharp inspection matters more than usual. It suits buyers who'd trade a builder warranty for tall ceilings and a story, and anyone who wants Decatur's square close enough to smell the biscuits.

highlights.title: Pink granite views
highlights.note: The courthouse anchors these blocks; half the streets frame it like a postcard.

highlights.title: Walkable errands
highlights.note: Coffee, boots, biscuits, and the full feed of small-town news, all on foot.

highlights.title: True Victorian stock
highlights.note: Gingerbread trim, deep porches, and floor plans with a century of opinions.

highlights.title: Front-row festivities
highlights.note: When Decatur celebrates on the square, this neighborhood is already there.

faq.q: Is the Square district a good place to live in Decatur?
faq.a: If you want walkability and character in a region where both are scarce, yes. You trade new-build convenience for porches, mature trees, and the courthouse square a stroll away. Homes are older and need attentive owners, but the neighborhood's rhythm — kids on bikes, neighbors on porches, events on the square — is exactly what people move to Decatur hoping to find.

faq.q: Which school district covers the Square district?
faq.a: Decatur ISD serves the neighborhoods around the courthouse square. It's the hometown district, which in a county-seat town means school events and square events tend to blur together in the best way. As always, confirm the assigned campuses for any specific address with the district before you write an offer.

faq.q: Are the homes near Decatur's square historic?
faq.a: Many of them, genuinely. These are the Victorian blocks that grew up around the courthouse, mixed with early bungalows and cottages added as the town filled in. Some are meticulously restored, others are still waiting their turn, so condition — foundations, wiring, plumbing — deserves a careful inspection. Buy the bones and the block; the charm is already included.

faq.q: How far is the Square district from Fort Worth or Dallas?
faq.a: Downtown Fort Worth runs about 38 minutes, mostly down US-287, and downtown Dallas is about 62. DFW Airport lands at about 48 minutes, with Legacy West in Plano about 56. That's the Decatur bargain: a real courthouse-square life on the metroplex's western edge, close enough for a commute, far enough that it still feels like the county seat it is.

faq.q: Can you walk to restaurants and shops from the Square district?
faq.a: That's the whole point. The square's cafes, boutiques, and boot-and-biscuit staples sit at the center of these blocks, and most houses put you within an easy stroll. In a region built around parking lots, a Decatur address where dinner and errands happen on foot is a genuinely rare thing in North Texas.

denton/landmark.tagline: Denton finally builds itself a big new neighborhood
intro: Big master plans usually happen where land is empty, which is exactly why Landmark is unusual: a genuinely large new community inside Denton proper — a city with a courthouse square, two universities, and an actual culture — rather than out where the map runs out of names.

That context is the sell. Buyers here get new-construction convenience without trading away the college-town texture: live music downtown, Saturday farmers markets, and a workforce anchor in the universities. The $400s entry band prices that combination against far more anonymous corners of the metro.
denton/landmark.homes: Landmark's MLS-matched inventory shows the deepest builder bench of any community we track in Denton — eight names including Drees, Perry, Tri Pointe, David Weekley, Coventry and Highland — from right-sized single-family plans to larger family footprints, opening in the $400s band.

highlights.title: City, not fringe
highlights.note: Inside Denton proper — square, universities, music halls — not a bare-field address.

highlights.title: Eight builders
highlights.note: The deepest MLS-observed builder mix we track in the city, with the plan variety to match.

highlights.title: The I-35 seam
highlights.note: Denton sits where I-35E and I-35W split, putting both halves of the metro in reach.

faq.q: Where is Landmark?
faq.a: Landmark is a new-build community inside Denton, Texas — the county seat and university town at the top of the metro where I-35 splits into its east and west branches.

faq.q: What do homes cost in Landmark?
faq.a: Active MLS-matched listings have recently opened in the $400s band. Verify current phases and pricing with the sales offices — releases move quickly in Denton's tight new-build market.

faq.q: Who is building in Landmark?
faq.a: Our MLS-matched listings show an unusually deep mix — Drees, Perry, Tri Pointe, David Weekley, Coventry, Highland and more. Treat the list as observed from listing data, not a definitive roster.

amenities: Amenity packages build out with the phases — confirm what's open today at the sales offices.
